NTSB:20260904203732.n: On September 3, 2026, about 0932 mountain standard time, a Bell OH-58, N480FT, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Deer Valley, Arizona. The pilots did not sustain any injuries. The helicopter was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight. The helicopter instructor reported he and a pilot-rated student departed from Phoenix Deer Valley Airport, Phoenix, Arizona to practice approaches, hovering autorotations, and autorotations with a power recovery in the local area. After completing the approaches and a hovering autorotation without incident, the instructor landed the helicopter and briefed the student about the autorotation with a power recovery procedure. Shortly after, the instructor and the student both demonstrated a successful autorotation with a power recovery. With the instructor on the controls and the helicopter about 500 ft above the ground (agl) and 70 knots indicating, the instructor initiated the third autorotation. The instructor noted that the entry was smooth and announced the main rotor rpm settled around 100% and that the N1 needle was around 62%, at idle engine power. About 200 ft agl and 60 knots, the instructor rolled the throttle to full power and joined the rotor rpm needle with the engine's rpm needle. As the helicopter crossed about 50 ft agl, the instructor initiated a flare and about 10-15 ft agl, he applied slight aft cyclic to slow the descent rate and terminate the recovery to a 3-5 ft agl hover. During the aft pitch control input, the low rotor RPM warning horn became audible and the instructor noted that he did not receive an engine response after he increased the throttle setting. The instructor quickly raised the collective lever to cushion the landing; however, the helicopter continued its descent and impacted terrain. Subsequently, the main rotor system separated from the mast and the helicopter sustained substantial damage to the fuselage, main rotor system, and drive train. The airplane was recovered to a secure facility for further examination.
NTSB:20260904203732.s: During a Part 91 instructional flight in a Bell OH-58, an instructor and student attempted an autorotation with power recovery. The helicopter impacted terrain near Deer Valley, Arizona, after the instructor received no engine response at 10–15 feet AGL, causing substantial damage and main rotor separation.

NTSB:20260904203733.n: On September 3, 2026, about 1518 mountain daylight time, a Cessna T206H airplane, N919CW, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Dunton, Colorado. The pilot and passenger were fatally injured. The flight was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 91 aerial survey flight. According to the operator the pilot and camera operator departed Grand Junction Regional Airport (GJT) Grand Junction, Colorado, completed their survey work and were returning to Belen Regional Airport (BRG) Belen, New Mexico, about 300 nautical miles south-southeast. The pilot was receiving VFR flight following from Denver Center and had been advised radio coverage may be intermitted due to the mountainous terrain. Review of preliminary automatic dependent system broadcast (ADS-B) data revealed the airplane departed GJT about 1341 and conducted aerial survey operations for about 45 minutes and then proceeded southeast between about 8,500 to 10,900 ft mean sea level (msl). The pilot’s route of flight took them slightly east of Dolores Peak, a 13,289 ft mountain with a ridgeline that extends from the peak to the east. On the flight earlier in the day from BRG to GJT the airplane passed over a ridgeline about 1.5 miles east of Dolores Peak, about 500 ft above ground level (agl). As the airplane approached Dolores Peak on the return flight, about 2 minutes from the ridgeline the airplane was about 500 ft agl and 101 knots. About 1 minute later and 1 mile from the accident site the airplane was 50 ft agl and 80 knots. At 1518 the airplane made a slight right turn and impacted trees and terrain. The final ADS-B target was located above the accident site. A hiker in the area stated that it was windier than normal the day of the accident. Figure 1 Preliminary Flight Track Data; Final segment of the accident flight track of N919CW with track details. The airplane impacted heavily wooded rising terrain in a wings level attitude at an elevation of 10,770 ft msl and was orientated on a 300° magnetic heading. The debris path was about 340 ft long and contained all major components of the airplane. The initial tree strike separated the left horizontal stabilizer. The left wing came to rest near the cockpit and fuselage. The right wing came to rest about 25 ft beyond the main wreckage. Flight control continuity was partially established; complete continuity could not be confirmed due to impact and thermal damage. Portions of the flight control cables were fragmented due to a large tree trunk; the breaks were consistent with impact overload. The engine was separated from its mounts and was located near the main wreckage and exhibited thermal damage. The propeller was separated from the engine; two of the three propeller blades were observed. One blade was straight, the other exhibited minor s-bending with a deep trailing edge gouge about mid-span of the de-ice boot. The wreckage was recovered and retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260904203733.s: A Cessna T206H conducting a Part 91 aerial survey flight impacted terrain near Dolores Peak, Colorado, killing the pilot and passenger. The aircraft descended to 50 feet AGL before striking trees and rising terrain while executing a slight right turn in windy conditions.

NTSB:20260904203734.n: On September 3, 2026, at 2004 eastern daylight time, a Piper PA-28-180, N7635W, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Dallas, Georgia. The flight instructor and student pilot were seriously injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight. The student pilot and flight instructor reported that the purpose of the flight was to perform practice takeoffs and landings at Paulding Northwest Atlanta Airport (PUJ), Dallas, Georgia. The student pilot arrived at the airport and performed a preflight inspection of the airplane. He sampled the fuel and found no contaminants, then checked its quantity with a fuel stick. He also checked the engine oil quantity and reported there were 6 quarts indicated on the oil dipstick. The flight instructor stated that he also checked the fuel and oil on the airplane and noted that there was nothing abnormal with the airplane. They then started the airplane and taxied to runway 13 for departure from PUJ. The student and flight instructor both stated that before departure, they performed an engine runup and did not notice anything abnormal. After departure they performed a series of uneventful touch-and-go landings at PUJ. During the accident touch-and-go, on initial climb the engine “cut out.” The flight instructor reported the airplane’s nose pitched down and the engine rpm abruptly dropped, but the propeller continued rotating. The student pilot reported that the flight instructor took control of the airplane and intended to land on a nearby road. Unable to reach that road, the flight instructor performed a forced landing in a densely wooded area. Preliminary review of ADS-B data showed that shortly after crossing the departure end of runway 13, and about 175 ft above ground level, the airplane turned left to the northeast. The airplane stopped climbing, continued to the northeast toward a road, and began descending. Just south of the road, the airplane turned east. Shortly thereafter ADS-B data showed no additional movement of the airplane. An on-scene examination by an FAA inspector found the airplane fuselage laying on its right side, with substantial damage, and both wings separated and suspended in trees. The airplane was equipped with avionics that were capable of recording flight data. They were recovered and sent to the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory for data download. The airplane’s most recent 100-hour inspection occurred on September 1, 2026. The accident flight was the fifth flight after that inspection. The wreckage was recovered and retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260904203734.s: During a touch-and-go practice flight in a Piper PA-28-180, the engine cut out on initial climb at 175 feet, causing the flight instructor to execute a forced landing in a wooded area. The accident resulted in substantial damage to the aircraft and serious injuries to the student pilot and flight instructor.

NTSB:20260904203738.n: On September 2, 2026, about 2007 central daylight time, a Six Chuter SR7XL experimental light-sport powered parachute, N5617X, was involved in an accident near Amery, Wisconsin. The pilot was seriously injured. The powered parachute was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot was conducting a post maintenance test flight after he had just completed a condition inspection on the powered parachute. During the inspection he had changed several hoses. The pilot told a witness the engine just quit. The powered parachute impacted trees while attempting to land and the pilot was seriously injured. The powered parachute was recovered and retained for further investigation.
NTSB:20260904203738.s: During a post-maintenance test flight of an SR7XL powered parachute, the engine quit after the pilot changed several hoses. The aircraft impacted trees during the landing attempt, resulting in serious injuries to the pilot.

NTSB:20260905203743.n: On September 5, 2026, about 1345 Pacific daylight time, a Grumman AA-5, N6510L, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Fresno, California. The pilot and 3 passengers were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. Surveillance video showed that the pilot and passengers boarded the airplane at the airplane owner’s residence at Sierra Sky Park Airport (E79), Fresno, California, and shortly after taxied to the approach end of runway 30. Another video showed the airplane begin its takeoff roll and subsequently abort the takeoff about halfway down the runway. The airplane continued down the runway, turned around at the departure end and taxied back to the runway approach end. At this time, the pilot texted the owner about a radio problem she was experiencing. About two minutes later the pilot taxied the airplane to the owner’s residence, which was located on the airport. According to text messages, the owner contacted a mechanic to troubleshoot the radio issue and a few minutes later the mechanic approached the airplane after it had been shut down. Shortly after, the airplane was observed taxiing towards the runway. According to witnesses located near the runway, the airplane taxied to the approach end of runway 30 and then started its takeoff roll. The airplane lifted off the runway about 1,000 ft from the departure end and pitched up hard into a nose-high attitude. Witnesses reported that the engine sounded weak and that there were no misfires or sputtering. The airplane continued down the runway at about 30 ft above ground level (agl). Surveillance video showed the airplane maintain a nose-high attitude about 30 ft agl as it overflew the remaining runway. A video, which captured the airplane further down the runway, showed it about 40 ft agl as it flew out of view in a nose-high attitude. The accident site was located in a washout at the top of sloping terrain, near impacted trees, about 1,000 ft northwest from the departure end of runway 30. The first identified point of contact was a large branch near the top of a 40 ft tree that had recently been topped to comply with FAA clearance regulations for the airport. Broken limbs and branches were spread out at the base of the impacted trees. The airplane came to rest upright in a washout near the impacted trees and was positioned on a magnetic heading of about 285°. The nose landing gear separated from the airplane and was found uphill in the washout near the impacted trees. The airplane was mostly consumed by postimpact fire. About an acre of surrounding terrain was burned by the fire. The wreckage was relocated to a secured facility for further examination.
NTSB:20260905203743.s: The pilot of a Grumman AA-5, N6510L, fatally injured herself and three passengers during a Part 91 takeoff from Fresno's Sierra Sky Park Airport. The aircraft pitched up hard with a weak engine sound, flew low in a nose-high attitude, and struck trees before being destroyed by postimpact fire.

NTSB:20260906203745.n: On September 5, 2026, about 2105 eastern daylight time, a Piper PA-28-181, N7653F, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Ludlow, Massachusetts. The pilot and passenger were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to preliminary ADS-B data, at 2054, the airplane departed from runway 14 at Northampton Airport (7B2), Northampton, Massachusetts, en route to Plymouth Municipal Airport (PYM), Plymouth, Massachusetts. Once clear of the runway, the airplane made a climbing left turn to a ground track of 088°. At 2056, the airplane turned right to 158° while continuing to climb to an altitude of 5,000 ft mean sea level (msl). During that time, the airplane made a series of slow left and right turns but remained relatively on course. At 2102, the airplane turned to about 180° and started to climb. Preliminary air traffic control information indicated that the controller at the Yankee Terminal Radar Approach Control contacted the pilot to inquire about the sudden turn to which the pilot responded that he was “correcting.” The airplane then began a climbing left turn to about 5,400 ft msl and a ground track of 023°. At 2103, the airplane began a right turn and spiral descent from an altitude of about 5,600 ft msl. The descent rate in the turn reached a rate of 11,520 feet per minute (fpm). As the turn tightened, the descent rate decreased to between 4,000 and 7,000 fpm and the airplane reached a maximum ground speed of 186 knots. The final ADS-B data point was recorded at 2104 at an altitude of 900 ft msl with a groundspeed of 162 knots, a vertical descent rate of 3,968 fpm and a ground track of 005°. The airplane impacted a wetland area 1,063 ft from the last recorded ADS-B data point. The wreckage path was oriented on a heading of 166° and was confined to an area 50 ft long by 30 ft wide. The airplane was severely fragmented and there was no post impact fire. The airplane wreckage was recovered and retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260906203745.s: A pilot and passenger were fatally injured when their Piper PA-28-181, N7653F, entered a spiral descent from 5,600 feet msl during a Part 91 flight near Ludlow, Massachusetts. The aircraft impacted a wetland area after the pilot reported "correcting" a sudden turn to air traffic control.

NTSB:20260906203747.n: On September 6, 2026, about 1353 eastern daylight time (EDT), 21 Air flight 7598, a Boeing 767-33A, N1997A, overran runway 30 after landing at Miami International Airport (MIA), Miami, Florida and subsequently impacted two ground passenger vehicles. The two crewmembers aboard the airplane sustained minor injuries. Five people on the ground sustained fatal injuries and three people on the ground sustained serious injuries. The airplane sustained substantial damage to include a postcrash fire on the right wing. Flight 7598 was a domestic cargo flight operating on behalf of Amazon.com Services LLC under the provisions of Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 121 from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport (SJU), San Juan, Puerto Rico, to MIA. In response to the accident, the NTSB traveled to MIA on September 7, 2026, to document the accident site and collect perishable evidence to support the investigation. As part of the investigative process, the NTSB invited qualified parties to participate in the investigation. These parties included the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), The Boeing Company, General Electric (GE) Aerospace, 21 Air, Miami-Dade Aviation Department (MDAD), National Air Traffic Controllers Association (NATCA), and 21 Air Pilots Association (TAPA). The parties were formed into specialized investigative groups led by NTSB group chairmen in the areas of Structures, Systems, Powerplants, Air Carrier Operations and Human Performance, Air Traffic Control (ATC), Airports and Survival Factors, Hazardous Materials, and Cockpit Voice Recorder (CVR). NTSB specialists for Meteorology and Aircraft Performance were on site to collect information in their respective fields. A Flight Data Recorder (FDR) specialist at the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory in Washington, DC conducted work on the FDR recovered from the accident airplane. NTSB Chairwoman Homendy was the Board Member on scene. History of Flight On the day of the accident, flight 7598 was the third flight for the accident airplane and the second flight for the accident flight crew. According to flight crew interviews, the captain and first officer (FO) reported for duty about 0530 EDT on the day of the accident. The accident flight crew flew the accident airplane from MIA to SJU as flight 7521, which departed MIA about 0635 EDT and landed in SJU about 0858 EDT. Flight 7521 was the first time the accident flight crew had flown together. For flight 7521, the FO was the pilot flying and the captain was the pilot monitoring. Flight 7598 departed SJU about 1124 EDT and was scheduled to arrive into MIA about 1428 EDT. For flight 7598, the captain was the pilot flying and the FO was the pilot monitoring. Flight 7598 was cleared for landing on runway 30 from MIA airport traffic control tower (ATCT)/terminal radar approach control (TRACON) about 1349 EDT when the airplane was about 12 nautical miles from the runway 30 displaced threshold. According to Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) Out and FDR data, flight 7598 was about 105 ft above ground level (agl) at a groundspeed of 177 kts as it crossed the threshold of runway 30. The accident airplane touched down about 3,750 ft past the threshold at a groundspeed of 160 kts. The airplane continued down runway 30, crossed the departure end of the runway at 113 kts, impacted the localizer and the Medium Intensity Approach Lighting System with Runway Alignment Indicator Lights (MALSR) at the northwest end of the runway at about 100kts, and departed the paved surface and onto the grass (see figure 1). The distance between the end of the paved surface to the location the accident airplane came to rest was about 1,200 ft. The last recorded groundspeed on the FDR was 65 kts, reached shortly after the accident airplane impacted an airport perimeter fence and traversed a public road (NW 67th Avenue). Prior to impacting the airport perimeter fence, the accident airplane impacted a Ford Econoline passenger van traveling on an airport perimeter road parallel to the perimeter fenceline (see figure 2). Of the seven occupants in the passenger van, five sustained fatal injuries and two sustained serious injuries. While traversing NW 67th avenue, the accident airplane impacted a Toyota Corolla Cross sport utility vehicle (SUV). The sole occupant in the SUV sustained serious injuries. The accident airplane impacted a chain link fence surrounding a parking lot and came to rest about 1,200 ft from the paved surface of runway 12/30. The captain egressed the airplane out of door 1L and the FO egressed out of the right cockpit window. About 1353 EDT, MIA ATCT/TRACON activated the alert phone in response to the accident. Miami-Dade Fire Rescue at MIA responded with 5 Aircraft Rescue and Fire Fighting (ARFF) units, with additional mutual aid resources dispatched following the initial response. Figure 1. NTSB aerial imagery superimposed on a satellite view of the area of the runway excursion. Figure 2. The impacted Ford Econoline van (left) and Toyota Corolla Cross SUV (right). Crew Experience The captain held an airline transport pilot certificate with a type rating for the Boeing 767 that he received on May 18, 2026. The captain was hired by 21 Air in April 2026. He had accrued about 7,267 total hours of flight experience, as reported in his interview with NTSB investigators, of which 150 hours were in the accident airplane make and model. The captain also had about 2,700 hours of flight experience in the Boeing 737. On September 5, 2026, the captain flew two flights comprising an outbound from MIA to El Dorado International Airport (BOG), Bogotá, Colombia, and a return flight from BOG to MIA. According to the operator’s records, the return flight departed BOG about 0441 EDT and arrived about 0902 EDT. The captain was subsequently off duty until the morning of the accident. The FO held an airline transport pilot certificate with a type rating for the Boeing 767 that he received on April 2, 2025. The FO was hired by 21 Air in February 2025. He had accrued about 2,800 total hours of flight experience, as reported in his interview with NTSB investigators, of which 800 hours were in the accident airplane make and model. The FO also had about 400 hours of flight experience on the McDonnell Douglas DC-9. On September 3, 2026, the FO flew two flights comprising an outbound from MIA to Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport (BWI), and a return flight from BWI to MIA. According to the operator’s records, the return flight departed BWI about 2209 EDT and arrived into MIA about 0033 EDT on September 4, 2026. The FO was subsequently off duty until the morning of the accident. Airplane and Operator Information The Boeing 767 is a two-engine widebody airplane that can be configured to carry passengers or cargo. The accident airplane was manufactured in June 1994 and was originally delivered as a passenger-carrying configuration. The airplane was subsequently converted to a freighter configuration in June 2016. The accident airplane was equipped with GE CF-6 engines. At the time of the accident, the airplane had accumulated a total time of about 110,077 flight hours and 24,505 flight cycles. 21 Air is a cargo airline with corporate headquarters in Greensboro, North Carolina, and operations based in Miami, Florida. At the time of the accident, the company operated 22 airplanes (including the accident airplane) composed of a mix of Boeing 757 and 767 airplanes. Meteorology An Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) is located at MIA. The main ASOS sensors are located near the approach end of runway 9, near taxiway S1, while additional ASOS sensors are located about 600 ft southeast of the accident site. At 1313 EDT, the MIA ASOS generated a Special Report (SPECI) that reported, in part, variable wind at 3 kts, visibility of 10 statute miles or greater, thunderstorms, scattered cumulonimbus clouds at 3,000 ft agl and broken ceiling at 5,000 ft agl. At 1337 EDT, the MIA ASOS reported a wind shift with the peak hourly wind occurring at 1352 EDT from 180° at 26 kts. At 1350 EDT, the MIA ASOS five-minute automated data reported, in part, winds at 190° at 16 kts with gusts to 24 kts. At 1353 EDT, the MIA ASOS generated an Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR) that reported, in part, wind from 190° at 17 kts with gusts to 26 kts, visibility of 10 statute miles or greater, thunderstorms, scattered cumulonimbus clouds at 2,000 ft agl, broken ceiling at 4,800 ft agl. Airport and ATC Information MIA is a major international airport for passenger and cargo operations. The airport operates four runways: 8L/26R, 8R/26L, 9/27, and 12/30 (see figure 3). All of the runways are asphalt and grooved. According to the FAA airport diagram for MIA, runway 12/30 measures 150 ft wide by 9,360 ft long, the length of which includes a displaced threshold for runway 30. Blast pads that are not considered part of the runway length are present at each end of runway. An engineered materials arresting system (EMAS) was not installed at the end of runway 30. Figure 3. FAA airport diagram for MIA. The MIA ATCT/TRACON is a combined tower and TRACON located west of the passenger terminal, between runways 9/27 and 12/30. The MIA TRACON personnel were responsible for approach and departure radar services for MIA, Fort Lauderdale/Hollywood International Airport (FLL), and surrounding satellite airports. The MIA tower personnel were responsible for air operations within a 6-mile radius of MIA, up to 1,000 ft agl, as well as ground movements on the airport surface area. The MIA ATCT local control north (LCN) controller was responsible for arrivals and departures on runways 8L/26R and 8R/26L while the local control south (LCS) controller was responsible for arrivals and departures on runways 9/27 and 12/30. The LCS on position at the time of the accident had a total of 11 years of experience in ATC and was certified for the LCS position in November 2019. At the time of the accident, the LCS was on position for about 17 minutes. The LCS issued a landing clearance to flight 7598 but did not issue information about the wind. Per FAA Order JO 7110.65BB, titled “Air Traffic Control,” both wind direction and velocity were required to be stated when authorizing use of a runway when a tailwind component exists. About 4 minutes prior to issuing the landing clearance to flight 7598, when asked by another flight for wind information, the LCS stated winds were from 190° at 19 kts with gusts to 22 kts. At the time of this wind advisory, flight 7598 was not on the LCS frequency. Flight Recorders The airplane was equipped with a CVR and a FDR, both of which were recovered from the accident airplane and transported to the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory in Washington, DC. Data from both the CVR and FDR were downloaded successfully. The CVR contained about 2 hours and 4 minutes of recorded data that included the accident flight. A summary of select events captured on the CVR during the final few minutes of the recording is provided in table 1. All times are referenced relative to the end of the CVR recording. Table 1. Select events captured on the CVR. Approximate Time to End of CVR Recording (mm:ss) Observation 06:02 The captain called for flaps to be set to 1 degree. 04:18 The flight crew checked in with Miami tower and were cleared to land on runway 30. 02:53 The captain called for flaps to be set to 5 degrees. 02:37 The flight crew lowered the landing gear. 02:14 The captain called for flaps to be set to 15 degrees. 01:42 The captain called for flaps to be set to 20 degrees, and the FO cautioned they were too fast. The FO made additional comments regarding the airplane’s excessive speed throughout the remainder of the recording. There was not a consistent verbal response to the comments about speed. 01:23 Sounds consistent with autopilot disconnect. 01:12 Electronic “one thousand” callout. 01:04 Electronic “sink rate sink rate” callout. 00:58 Electronic “five hundred” callout. 00:57 Electronic “sink rate sink rate” callout. 00:54 Electronic “one hundred” callout. 00:50 Electronic “minimums” callout. 00:48 Electronic “too low terrain” callout. Annunciated four times. 00:41 The captain called for flaps to be set to 30 degrees. 00:40 Electronic “forty” callout. 00:39 Electronic “too low terrain” callout. 00:36 Electronic “ten” callout. 00:31 Sounds similar to the airplane touching down. 00:15 The captain called for a go-around. 00:10 Sounds similar to the airplane departing the paved surface. 00:00 The CVR recording ended. The FDR contained about 54 hours of data that spanned 16 flights, including the accident flight. The FDR recorded more than 400 parameters of flight data. Figure 4 shows a plot of the FDR data from 1350 EDT, when flight 7598 was about 9.8 nautical miles from the threshold of runway 30, until the end of recorded data. Figure 5 shows a plot of the FDR data from 1352:25, when flight 7598 was about 1.5 nautical miles from the threshold of runway 30, until the end of recorded data. Left and right main landing gear tire contact marks on runway 30 were found about 3,750 ft and 3,820 ft, respectively, from the threshold of the approach end of runway 30. According to FDR data, the airplane’s groundspeed was about 160 kts at the location of these initial tire contact marks, about 13 seconds after flight 7598 crossed the runway 30 threshold. The landing gear weight-on-wheels (WOW) parameter intermittently switched between “air” to “ground” for about 7 seconds. The WOW parameter switched to ground for the remainder of the recorded data when the airplane had about 2,730 ft of runway remaining. The FDR data showed the speed brakes remained stowed and the thrust reversers did not deploy during the landing and subsequent landing rollout. Wheel brakes were manually applied at a groundspeed of 146 kts. The brake pedals for wheel braking were subsequently released about 8 seconds later at a groundspeed of 120 kts and the throttle resolver angle for both engines increased to go-around thrust values; the airplane had about 930 ft of runway remaining. About 4 seconds later, the throttle resolver angles for both engines reduced to idle values at a groundspeed of 117 kts, when wheel brakes were reapplied; the airplane had about 415 ft of runway remaining. The airplane departed the runway at a groundspeed of 113 kts and subsequently impacted the localizer and MALSR at the northwest end of runway 30. FDR and other engineering data will be incorporated into an NTSB airplane performance study to refine this preliminary sequence of events and to analyze the physical state of the airplane during its approach and landing on runway 30. Figure 4. FDR data for the accident flight from 13:50:00 until the end of recorded data. Figure 5. FDR data for the accident flight from 1352:25 until the end of recorded data. Wreckage Examination The accident airplane came to rest on an area of grass to the west of NW 67th Avenue and adjacent to a parking lot. Ground impressions consistent with the nose, right main, and left main landing gear were found along the path of the airplane departing from runway 12/30 to where the airplane came to rest (see figure 6). The nose landing gear was found displaced aft and was found underneath the belly of the airplane. The left and right main landing gear assemblies were found in an extended and locked landing configuration. Measurement of the brake wear pins on both the left and right main landing gear found all wear pins showed remaining service life for all eight wheels. Figure 6. An aerial view of N1997A showing the relative location of the two impacted ground vehicles and ground scars leading up to the airplane’s resting location. Several orange paint transfer marks were found on the fuselage, wing leading edge, and horizontal stabilizer leading edge, consistent with the airplane impacting the localizer and MALSR at the northwest end of runway 30. The inboard end of the right wing remained attached to the fuselage and exhibited varying amounts of heat damage from the postcrash fire. Portions of the right wing were thermally deformed downward with its outboard end resting on the ground. A large section of the upper wing skin had separated from the right wing and was found in the adjacent parking lot, about 158 ft to the northwest of the airplane. The right engine was thermally damaged, partially separated from the wing pylon structure, oriented outboard of its normally installed position, and was resting on the ground. In the cockpit, the flap lever was found in the 25° detent (see figure 7). Measurement of the left- and right-wing slat tracks and flap support rods were consistent with a flaps 25° setting. The throttle levers were found in the idle position, and the fuel control switches were found in the cut-off position. Both engine fire handles were up and rotated and the auxiliary power unit (APU) fire handle was down. The thrust reverser levers were found in the first detent position. The speed brake lever was in the down (stowed) position. Figure 7. The cockpit center aisle stand with the position of various controls observed at the accident site. The NTSB’s investigation of 21 Air flight 7598 is ongoing.
NTSB:20260906203747.s: 21 Air Flight 7598, a Boeing 767 cargo flight, overran runway 30 at Miami International Airport after landing at 160 knots and impacting two ground vehicles, killing five people. The aircraft sustained substantial damage and a postcrash fire while the two crewmembers suffered minor injuries.

NTSB:20260907203748.n: On September 7, 2026, about 1015 eastern daylight time, a Mooney M20F airplane, N9546M, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Titusville, Florida. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. Airplane position data revealed that the flight departed from runway 36 (taxiway Charlie intersection) at the Space Coast Regional Airport (TIX), Titusville, Florida. About 1015:07, the airplane overflew the departure end of the runway. About that time, it entered a left turn and climbed to a maximum altitude of about 220 ft mean sea level (msl). The left turn continued until the final data point was recorded at 1015:27. The altitude associated with the final data point was 220 ft msl, and the airplane was oriented on a southwest heading at that time. Surveillance video footage from a camera located at the Executive Jet Center fixed base operator depicted the airplane as it departed. Initially, the airplane became airborne and began to climb. However, soon afterward, it entered a descent. As it neared the end of the runway, the airplane began to climb again and subsequently entered a left turn. The turn continued until the airplane ultimately descended behind an intervening tree line. Shortly afterward, a plume of smoke was visible rising above the trees. A witness positioned outside the museum on the east side of the airport reported observing the airplane. Initially, she thought that the pilot was descending to execute a touch-and-go but then the airplane started to climb. She noted “a lot of noise” from the airplane as it climbed; however, that noise stopped shortly afterward as it neared the end of the runway. The airplane then entered a left turn and, ultimately, impacted power lines. The airplane struck a set of powerlines before coming to rest inverted on the westbound traffic lanes of Route 405/Columbia Blvd immediately north of the airport property. A post-impact fire ensued. The accident site was about 0.29 miles northwest from the departure end of runway 36. Figure 1 – Aerial view of accident site The cockpit area, including the instrumentation and avionics, was consumed. The outboard section to the left wing was separated and located near the main wreckage consistent with the powerline impact. The aft fuselage was deformed and buckled that was consistent with impact forces. The empennage remained attached with exception of the upper 2-ft section of the rudder which was separated and located in the debris path. The nose landing gear and left main landing gear were in the extended position. The right main landing gear was separated and located in the debris path. Figure 2 – Airplane at accident site
NTSB:20260907203748.s: A pilot operating a Mooney M20F on a Part 91 personal flight was fatally injured when the aircraft impacted power lines shortly after departing Titusville's Runway 36. The airplane entered a left turn at 220 feet, descended behind a tree line, struck power lines, and caught fire.

NTSB:20260907203749.n: On September 7, 2026, about 1337 central daylight time, an experimental STOL CH701 airplane, N101XV, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Neosho, Missouri. The pilot and passenger sustained fatal injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 91 personal flight. According to a friend, the pilot had flown to the Neosho Hugh Robinson Airport (EOS), Neosho, Missouri, to assist him with some airplane maintenance. The maintenance consisted of temporarily removing and installing the accident airplane airspeed indicator into another airplane to allow for a ferry flight. After that ferry flight, the airspeed indicator was reinstalled and “tested” in the accident airplane. The pilot departed in the accident airplane with another friend about 1334. A witness reported that the airplane departed EOS with no issues observed during the takeoff or initial climb. After he observed the initial climb, he got back into his vehicle and did not observe any further portion of the flight. At 1335:39, a dash camera video recording, positioned about 0.80 nautical miles east of the airport, captured the airplane on the left crosswind for runway 19. The airplane tracked west to east before starting a left turn toward the northwest at about 1335:47. At 1335:50, the recording showed an unknown object departing and falling away from the airplane. The airplane continued the left turn and entered a nose down descent before disappearing behind a tree line. The accident site was located in an open field about 0.48 nautical miles east of the departure end of runway 19. Impact ground scars and debris were consistent with the airplane impacting terrain in a nearly vertical nose down attitude (see figure 1). Figure 1. Accident site overview Postaccident examination revealed that the left inboard leading-edge PegaSTOL slat was separated and not found within the vicinity of the main wreckage. The PegaSTOL wing slat system is manufactured by Dédalius Aviation Inc. A couple of days after the accident, the leading-edge slat was found by law enforcement about 0.14 nautical miles southwest of the accident site (see figure 2). Figure 2. Left inboard leading-edge slat. The airplane was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260907203749.s: The pilot and passenger of an experimental CH701 sustained fatal injuries when the aircraft crashed shortly after departing Neosho Airport. Post-accident examination revealed the left inboard leading-edge slat separated in flight, causing a nose-down descent and impact.

NTSB:20260908203750.n: On September 7, 2026, about 1720 Pacific daylight time, a Cessna 172N, N734ZK, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near San Diego, California. The flight instructor and student pilot were fatally injured. The airplane was being operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight. Preliminary ADS-B data showed the airplane departed Montgomery-Gibbs Executive Airport (MYF), San Diego, California about 1615. The airplane remained in the local airport traffic pattern for the duration of the accident flight, performing nine left-hand visual traffic patterns to runway 28L. Airport and nearby business security cameras captured portions of the accident flight as the airplane approached the runway and as the pilots performed multiple go around maneuvers. Witnesses also observed the airplane and described the airplane as flying very erratically during multiple go-around maneuvers, pitching upward steeply after the go-around was initiated, flying very slow, and “stalling” before the airplane recovered. On the nineth approach the airplane can be seen in one of the videos flying low near the ground as it approached the runway, nosing over, pitching up and then nosing over a second time. The airplane then entered a steep nose high pitch attitude prior to the runway 28L threshold. The airplane appeared to attain about 45° pitch up attitude while about 100 to 200 ft above ground level. The airplane entered a steep left descending turn and impacted runway 28L near the runway threshold. The airplane came to rest on taxiway B and a post impact fire ensued. The wreckage was examined on scene. The fuselage, inboard wings, and cowling sustained heavy thermal damage. The inboard sections of both wing fuel tanks were partially consumed by fire. All primary flight controls were identified at the accident site. Flight control continuity was confirmed from the cockpit controls to each flight control surface. The engine was examined and the crankshaft was rotated in its normal direction of rotation. Thumb compression was obtained on all four cylinders. Equal movement of all intake and exhaust rocker arms was observed on all cylinders. The aluminum fixed pitch 2-blade propeller remained attached to the crankshaft propeller flange. Blade “A” exhibited rearward bending and torsional twisting along its blade length with its tip missing. Blade “B” was mostly thermally consumed by the post impact fire. Two sections of propeller tip were found between the initial impact marks and the main wreckage. Each portion of blade tip found was twisted, fractured, and heavily scored. No anomalies were identified that would have precluded the normal production of engine power.
NTSB:20260908203750.s: A flight instructor and student pilot were fatally injured when their Cessna 172N crashed near San Diego during a Part 91 instructional flight. The aircraft entered a steep nose-high attitude and descending turn after erratic go-arounds, impacting Runway 28L and burning, with no pre-accident engine anomalies found.

NTSB:20260908203752.n: On September 7, 2026, about 1248 central daylight time, a Cessna 337C airplane, N2657S, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Brenham, Texas. The pilot sustained minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 post-maintenance test flight. According to the pilot, who is also a mechanic, he had recently purchased the push-pull configuration airplane on September 3, 2026. The airplane had been based for the last several years with the previous owner at the Brenham Municipal Airport (11R), Brenham, Texas. According to the aviation operations manager at 11R, he refueled the airplane prior to the flight. All four of the fuel tanks were topped off with 100 low lead fuel and he ensured the four fuel tank caps were all secured. The pilot reported there were no issues noted during the runup sequence. The airplane taxied from the ramp to runway 16 for the local area flight. During the takeoff sequence, the pilot reported the rear engine sustained a total loss of power at the point of rotation. The pilot performed a forced landing on a ranching property, about 0.85 miles to the southeast of the departure end of runway 16. The airplane came to rest upright on a flat grass field, right next to a metal fence and barn. The airplane sustained substantial damage to both wings, the fuselage, and the empennage. The airplane is pending recovery from the accident site to a secure location for future examination. The airplane, which is known as a Super Skymaster, was built in 1968. The airplane was equipped with front and rear Continental Motors IO-360-C reciprocating engines and McCauley Propeller Systems D2AF34C59 (front) and McCauley Propeller Systems D2AF34C61 (rear) two-blade aluminum propellers. According to the meteorological reporting station located at 11R, the calculated density altitude near the time of the accident was 2,571 ft.
NTSB:20260908203752.s: During a Part 91 post-maintenance test flight of a Cessna 337C, the pilot-mechanic experienced a total loss of rear engine power at rotation. He executed a forced landing on a nearby ranch, resulting in substantial damage to the aircraft and minor injuries.

NTSB:20260908203753.n: On September 6, 2026, about 1800 Pacific daylight time, an experimental Pitts Model 12 airplane, N491X, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Lake Stevens, Washington. The pilot sustained serious injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to the pilot, after departing Frontier Air Park (WN53), Lake Stevens, Washington, he began practicing a series of aerobatic maneuvers in the vicinity of the airport. During a spin, the airplane experienced what the pilot described as a partial loss of engine power. After recovering from the spin, the pilot applied full power, but the engine did not respond. The pilot attempted to troubleshoot by activating the electric boost pump; however, the engine remained at idle power. The pilot stated that he determined he would not reach the runway and aimed for a treed area between two homes. The pilot further stated that, while attempting to extend the airplane's glide at low altitude, the airplane subsequently entered a right spin. The pilot reported that he regained control of the airplane, rolled the wings level, and flared before impacting terrain. Multiple witnesses captured video of the accident sequence and the aerobatic maneuvers that preceded the accident. The videos show the accident airplane recover from a series of spins at a low altitude, make a right turn, and fly wings level for several seconds before entering another spin and descending below the tree line. The propeller can be seen rotating, and engine noise is audible throughout the recorded accident sequence. Figure Accident airplane at accident site (NTSB Photo) The airplane impacted a treed area between two homes and came to rest on its left side (see figure), which resulted in substantial damage to the wings and fuselage. The wreckage was recovered to a secure facility for further examination.
NTSB:20260908203753.s: The pilot of an experimental Pitts Model 12 sustained serious injuries when the aircraft was substantially damaged during low-altitude aerobatics near Lake Stevens, Washington. The pilot reported a partial engine power loss during a spin, failed to regain power, and subsequently entered another spin before impacting a treed area.

NTSB:20260908203754.n: On September 8, 2026, about 1100 central daylight time, a Boeing-Stearman A75L300 airplane, N680HW, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Bogue Chitto, Mississippi. The pilot sustained minor injuries and the passenger was uninjured. The airplane operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot reported that in cruise flight, the passenger reported that oil spray was coming in the cockpit and he could smell burning oil from the engine. The pilot saw that oil pressure had decreased and began to divert to the nearest airfield. When the oil pressure read zero, the pilot shut the engine down and performed a forced landing on a road. During the landing, the airplane's lower right wing collided with a road sign, and the pilot subsequently lost control of the airplane. The airplane then turned and veered through a fence and came to rest in a pasture. During the accident sequence, the fuselage and the upper and lower wings sustained substantial damage. A visual inspection of the engine by responding FAA inspectors did not locate an obvious source for the reported loss of oil. The airplane was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260908203754.s: The pilot of a Boeing-Stearman A75L300 reported oil spray and zero oil pressure in cruise, forcing a road landing where the wing struck a sign, causing loss of control and substantial damage. FAA inspectors found no obvious source for the oil loss during their visual inspection.

NTSB:20260908203757.n: The flight instructor and the student pilot were practicing touch-and-go landings. According to the instructor, the student landed flat and bounced. The landing had enough force that the airplane ballooned back into the air and began to veer to the right of the runway centerline. The instructor told the student to use full power and abort the landing. The student only applied 30 to 50% power and the airplane continued to veer to the right. The instructor told the instructor to again use full power, but it was too late and the airplane veered off the right side of the runway, hit a bump, and nosed over into the grass resulting in substantial damage to the fuselage. The instructor reported that there were no mechanical deficiencies of the airplane that contributed to the accident, and that he should have taken control from the student sooner to prevent the airplane from going off the runway.
NTSB:20260908203757.s: A flight instructor and student pilot practicing touch-and-go landings experienced a bounce that caused the aircraft to veer right. The student applied insufficient power to abort, resulting in the airplane leaving the runway, hitting a bump, and nosing over with substantial fuselage damage.

NTSB:20260909203759.n: On September 5, 2026, at 1422 eastern daylight time, a Bell 47G-4A, N797WS, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Alcoma, Florida. The pilot was not injured. The helicopter was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot reported that about 43 minutes after takeoff, he felt the helicopter momentarily yaw to the left twice. About 10 seconds later he heard a brief "metallic grinding noise," which was followed by a loss of altitude, at which point the pilot performed a forced landing. The helicopter came to rest in trees resulting in substantial damage to the engine mounts, pitch change linkage, and tailboom. The helicopter was recovered and retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260909203759.s: The pilot of a Bell 47G-4A helicopter reported a left yaw and metallic grinding noise during a Part 91 personal flight, causing a loss of altitude and forced landing. The aircraft sustained substantial damage to the engine mounts, pitch change linkage, and tailboom after coming to rest in trees.

NTSB:20260909203766.n: On September 7, 2026, about 1255 eastern daylight time, a Cirrus Design Corp SR22, N521LM, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Ashland, Ohio. The pilot was not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot stated that during landing at Ashland County Airport (3G4), Ashland, Ohio, the airplane's right brake did not operate. The left brake operated normally, and the airplane began to veer to the left. He kept the airplane on the centerline of the runway utilizing rudder controls; however, when the airplane slowed down it departed the left side of the runway and contacted two runway lights, which resulted in substantial damage to the wing and firewall. Examination of the airplane by an FAA inspector revealed that the right brake disc was circumferentially fractured. The brake disc was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260909203766.s: During landing at Ashland County Airport, a Cirrus SR22 pilot reported right brake failure causing the aircraft to veer left and depart the runway. The plane struck two runway lights, sustaining substantial wing and firewall damage due to a circumferentially fractured right brake disc.

NTSB:20260910203775.n: The pilot stated that during approach and landing in the tailwheel equipped airplane he was flying into the sun, which limited his vision. He also described that the wind was almost direct crosswind and shifting. The pilot further stated that he should have conducted a go-around because the airplane was unforgiving at lower airspeeds. Upon touchdown, the airplane landed on the main landing gear firmly and the airplane bounced before becoming airborne again. As the pilot was attempting to land the airplane again, the pilot thought the wind was pushing the airplane to the left. He attempted to compensate with right brake and lost directional control, resulting in a runway excursion into the soft ground. The airplane nosed over and came to rest inverted resulting in substantial damage to the right wing and vertical stabilizer. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260910203775.s: The pilot of a tailwheel airplane lost directional control during a landing in shifting crosswinds and sun glare, causing a runway excursion. The aircraft bounced, nosed over, and came to rest inverted with substantial damage to the right wing and vertical stabilizer.

NTSB:20260910203778.n: On September 8, 2026, about 0044 mountain daylight time, N393JW, a Beech 200, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Roswell, New Mexico. The two pilots and two of the medical crew members were not injured, a third medical crew member received minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 135 Air Medical flight. The airplane departed Albuquerque International Sunport (ABQ), Albuquerque, New Mexico, about 2350, on an instrument flight rules (IFR) flight plan to Roswell Air Center (ROW), Roswell, New Mexico. According to the pilots, the pilot flying was performing his initial operating experience (IOE) flight, the pilot observing was evaluating the IOE flight, and the flight had been uneventful. A stable approach to runway 17 was flown, and both pilots confirmed seeing 3 green landing gear down indicator lights. The pilots stated that the airplane crossed the runway threshold at 110 kts and the pilot flying began the airplane’s landing flare. The airplane touched down harder and sooner than he expected, and the airplane bounced. During the bounce, the airplane began to roll to the left, and the pilot observing announced, “my controls.” The pilot observing assumed control of the airplane, leveled the wings, and reestablished the airplane’s landing flare. During the second landing flare, the pilot observing (now flying) retracted the flaps “to settle the aircraft”, and thought the airplane was rolling on its landing gear. The airplane continued to sink toward the runway and the pilots subsequently heard the fuselage scraping the pavement. The pilot observing (now flying) secured the engines to assist with slowing the airplane, and it came to a stop about 1/3rd down the length of the runway. Postaccident examination of the airplane revealed that both main landing gear were collapsed, and the lower fuselage sustained substantial damage. The wreckage was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260910203778.s: During an IOE Part 135 air medical landing of a Beech 200 at Roswell, the aircraft bounced and rolled left after a hard touchdown. The pilot observing retracted flaps to settle the aircraft, causing the fuselage to scrape the runway and both main landing gear to collapse.

NTSB:20260910203785.n: While enroute, the pilot elected to divert the flight to an airport that was equipped with a single 2,129 ft-long runway. The pilot described a normal approach over trees at the approach end of the runway and that the airplane touched down about ¼ of the way down the runway. About mid-field, he stated that he did not feel that the airplane was slowing normally. He elected not to abort the landing and applied maximum braking. The airplane departed the right side of the runway before passing the runway end and rolling down an embankment and through a wooden fence. The engine mount was substantially damaged during the accident sequence. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation, nor were any discrepancies of the airplane's flaps or brakes discovered during a postaccident examination.
NTSB:20260910203785.s: The pilot diverted to an airport with a 2,129 ft runway and landed normally but felt insufficient deceleration mid-field. Despite applying maximum braking, the aircraft overran the right side, rolled down an embankment, and sustained substantial engine mount damage with no mechanical failures found.

NTSB:20260910203790.n: On September 10, 2026, about 1005 mountain daylight time, a Cessna 210, N9517T, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Polson Airport (8S1), Polson, Montana. The student pilot was not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight The pilot reported that he was returning to 8S1 after a short flight. The flight was uneventful until the airplane was on final approach. According to the pilot, the airplane was high on the approach, and he initiated a forward slip to increase the descent rate. About 20 to 30 seconds after entering the slip, the engine lost all power. The propeller continued to windmill during the descent The pilot verified the mixture and fuel selector positions and manipulated the throttle; however, he was unsuccessful in his attempt to restore engine power. The pilot discontinued the slip and established a glide toward the airport. The airplane crossed a road near the approach end of the runway and struck a fence before coming to rest on the airport grass. The lower fuselage and left wing were substantially damaged during the accident sequence. The pilot reported that each wing tank contained about 16 gallons of fuel before departure. Fuel samples were obtained from the airplane, and the airplane was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260910203790.s: A student pilot flying a Cessna 210 on final approach to Polson Airport (8S1) experienced a total engine power loss while performing a forward slip. Despite unsuccessful attempts to restore power, the pilot glided the aircraft to a forced landing, striking a fence and sustaining substantial damage to the lower fuselage and left wing.

NTSB:20260911203796.n: The pilot stated that during the takeoff roll a wind gust lifted the upwind wing and the nose gear off the runway, after which the airplane became airborne and entered a left bank. The pilot was unable to regain control, and the airplane subsequently impacted the ground. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical failures or malfunctions with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation. The pilot stated that he observed a right-quartering surface wind of about 7 knots and a dissipating thunderstorm near the airport during the takeoff roll. A review of the weather information revealed active convective weather with precipitation echoes about 6 miles southeast of the accident site. Wind was reported as 070° at 6 knots. Based on the available weather information, it is likely that convective outflow associated with the nearby thunderstorm produced the wind gust encountered by the airplane during takeoff.
NTSB:20260911203796.s: The pilot reported that a wind gust from a nearby thunderstorm lifted the aircraft's upwind wing and nose gear during takeoff, causing an uncontrolled left bank and ground impact. The airplane sustained substantial fuselage damage, with no pre-accident mechanical failures identified.

NTSB:20260914203805.n: On September 10, 2026, about 1545 eastern daylight time, a Beech 99 airplane, N799CZ, and a Diamond DA20 airplane, N84VV were involved in a ground collision accident at the Willow Run Airport, Belleville, Michigan. N799CZ received minor damage and N84VV received substantial damage. There were no injuries to either the pilot of N799CZ, or the student pilot and flight instructor on-board N84VV. N799CZ was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 135 cargo flight, and N84VV was operated as a Title 14 CFR Part 91 instructional flight. The pilot of N799CZ reported that after starting the airplane's engines, he set the parking brake and then turned around to turn on the airplane's oxygen bottle which was located behind his seat. While turned he noticed what he thought was a loose cargo strap but discovered that the strap was not loose. When he turned back around the airplane had moved and the propellers began striking the tail of the other airplane. He stopped and shut down the airplane. Both the flight instructor and student pilot of N84VV reported that they had completed their preflight inspection of N84VV and had started the airplane's engine and were stationary. As they were preparing to taxi, they felt the airplane getting struck by N799CZ. They noted that they did not see N799CZ from the cockpit before the collision. Following the collision, they shut down the airplane and deplaned. N84VV received substantial damage to the left horizontal stabilizer, left elevator, vertical stabilizer, rudder, left wing flap and left wing aileron.
