NTSB:20260914203805.s: A Beech 99 cargo pilot and a Diamond DA20 instructor with a student were involved in a ground collision at Willow Run Airport while both aircraft were stationary. The Beech 99 moved after the pilot turned to check an oxygen bottle, causing its propellers to strike the Diamond's tail, resulting in substantial damage to the Diamond and minor damage to the Beech with no injuries.

NTSB:20260914203807.n: On September 13, 2026, about 1515 Pacific daylight time, a Cessna P210N airplane, N4617W, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near San Luis Obispo, California. The pilot, pilot-rated-passenger, and a passenger were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot reported that the flight originated from Van Nuys Airport (VNY) Van Nuys, California and was destined for San Luis Obispo County Regional Airport (SBP) San Luis Obispo, California, where the pilot planned to conduct a practice area navigation (RNAV) GPS runway 29 approach. After the airplane touched down on the runway, the main landing gear collapsed; the left elevator and horizontal stabilizer were substantially damaged. The pilot reported that, when he extended the landing gear, he saw that the green landing gear advisory light was illuminated and the main landing gear was moving. The airplane came to rest upright on the runway. The main landing gear was partially extended, and the nose gear remained down and locked. The airplane was recovered to a secure location for further examination.
NTSB:20260914203807.s: The pilot of a Cessna P210N reported that the main landing gear collapsed upon touchdown at San Luis Obispo County Regional Airport during a Part 91 flight. Although the green gear light was on and the gear appeared to be moving, the main gear was only partially extended, causing substantial damage to the left elevator and horizontal stabilizer.

NTSB:20260914203810.n: On September 11, 2026 about 0830 eastern daylight time, a Robinson R44 helicopter, N4026E, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Colquitt, Georgia. The pilot was not injured. The helicopter was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 137 agricultural flight. According to the pilot, he completed a preflight inspection and engine run-up of the helicopter and found no anomalies. He verified all gauges were in the green and hovered the helicopter over to a trailer and landed on the trailer. Ground personnel added five gallons of fuel and loaded 50 lbs of liquid to the helicopter while the helicopter remained running. The ground personnel unhooked all the hoses from the helicopter and gave the pilot a signal it was safe to depart from the trailer. The pilot lifted the helicopter to a hover over the trailer and verified all gauges were still in the green. The pilot pushed forward on the cyclic to depart from the trailer, as the helicopter began to move forward, he felt a jolt and heard and felt the engine "skipping." Subsequently the engine lost partial power and the helicopter settled into the terrain resulting in a hard landing. The helicopter sustained substantial damage to the tail boom, tail rotor gear box, and tail rotor blades. A detailed wreckage examination is pending.
NTSB:20260914203810.s: The pilot of a Robinson R44 helicopter operating a Part 137 agricultural flight experienced partial engine power loss and a hard landing shortly after departing a fueling trailer. The accident caused substantial damage to the tail boom, tail rotor gearbox, and blades, though the pilot was not injured.

NTSB:20260914203813.n: The pilot of the retractable-landing-gear airplane reported that, following takeoff, the landing gear failed to retract when commanded. Multiple attempts to cycle the landing gear were unsuccessful, leading the pilot to suspect a malfunction within the hydraulic system, possibly involving the hydraulic pump. The pilot elected to leave the landing gear extended and return for landing. Prior to landing, all three landing gear indicated down and locked through both the primary electrical indication system and the secondary mechanical indicators (barber pole indicators located on the wings and nose). In addition, a visual inspection conducted by a pilot in a nearby airplane confirmed that all three landing gear appeared to be in the down-and-locked position. The landing and subsequent rollout were uneventful until the aircraft decelerated to approximately 60 knots and began moving toward the left side of the runway in accordance with racing procedures. At that time, the right main landing gear collapsed, the right wing contacting the runway surface and the airplane subsequently departed the runway. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the right wing. Post-accident examination of the airplane’s hydraulic system revealed no mechanical malfunctions or failures that would have precluded normal operation. Examination of the airplane’s electrical system revealed that the battery was in a low-charge condition. Testing showed that battery voltage decreased from about 19 volts to 11 volts when the electrically driven hydraulic pump was activated. Further inspection identified a failed reverse-current diode that prevented the generator from recharging the battery during operation. The airplane was routinely started using a ground power unit and the battery was not being fully recharged between flights. As a result, insufficient system voltage was available to adequately power the hydraulic pump, which prevented normal landing gear retraction and extension.
NTSB:20260914203813.s: The pilot of a retractable-landing-gear airplane reported a gear retraction failure after takeoff caused by a failed reverse-current diode and low battery voltage. Although the gear appeared locked, the right main gear collapsed during rollout, causing the wing to strike the runway and the aircraft to depart the surface with substantial damage.

NTSB:20260914203814.n: The pilot reported that he completed a preflight inspection, then departed on a local personal flight. During the flight, he contacted and invited three people for a local sightseeing flight. He estimated the weights of each passenger and believed the helicopter would be under the maximum gross weight for the passenger flight. The pilot loaded the heaviest passenger up front and the other two in the rear seats. During takeoff, as he applied throttle and collective the helicopter became light on its skids and all engine indications were normal. Immediately after the helicopter became airborne, it pitched nose down and accelerated forward. Despite subsequent control inputs, the pilot was unable to arrest the helicopter's forward motion and descent, which resulted in the main rotor blade and right skid contacting the ground. The helicopter came to rest on its right side, and the main rotor blades, fuselage, and tailboom were substantially damaged during the accident sequence. The pilot stated that after the accident he calculated the weight and balance and determined that the helicopter's center of gravity was beyond the forward limit. He reported that during the flight just prior to picking up the passengers, there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the helicopter that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260914203814.s: The pilot of a helicopter departed for a local sightseeing flight with three passengers, estimating the weight was within limits. The aircraft pitched nose down immediately after takeoff due to a center of gravity beyond the forward limit, resulting in a crash with substantial damage to the rotor, fuselage, and tailboom.

NTSB:20260914203817.n: On September 13, 2026, about 0930 central daylight time, a Vans Aircraft Inc, RV-4, N254MM, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Harrisonville, Missouri. The pilot and passenger were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot reported that while cruising at 5,500 ft mean sea level and 152 knots, about 5 to 10 miles south of Lawrence Smith Memorial Airport (LRY), Harrisonville, Missouri, the canopy unlatched warning light began to intermittently illuminate and extinguish. A few seconds after, the airplane was substantially damaged when the canopy separated from the airplane. The pilot executed a 180° turn and landed without further incident at LRY. The canopy was subsequently located about 5.3 nautical miles southeast of LRY. The airplane and canopy were retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260914203817.s: The pilot of a Vans RV-4 reported that while cruising at 5,500 feet near Harrisonville, Missouri, the canopy unlatched warning light illuminated intermittently before the canopy separated. The pilot executed a 180° turn and landed safely at Lawrence Smith Memorial Airport with no injuries, though the aircraft was substantially damaged.

NTSB:20260915203819.n: On September 15, 2026, about 0620 central daylight time, an experimental amateur-built RV-4, N469TW, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Albertville, Alabama. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The airplane was based at the pilot’s residence on a private airport. A witness near the airport reported that they saw the airplane being taxied to the south end of the runway before it departed to the northeast at about sunrise. An additional witness near the accident site reported that the airplane overflew her residence in a steep left bank and its associated engine noise caused her windows to rattle. She stated that the airplane narrowly missed trees and utility lines along a roadway and that the airplane remained in the left bank as it descended and impacted the ground; a postimpact fire ensued. The accident site was located about 75 ft east of the private airport’s runway in a wooded area that bordered an open field area near the base of a water tower. The wreckage path was about 382 ft-long and oriented on a magnetic heading of 024° at an elevation of 1,150 ft. The first identified point of impact was a linear ground scar about 27 ft-long that contained the left wingtip navigation light lens and fragments of the left wingtip. A soil depression observed at the end of the ground scar contained the fragmented engine cowlings and sections of the engine’s exhaust system. The main wreckage came to rest in an upright position about 102 ft from the initial point of impact and was oriented on magnetic heading of 030°. The postimpact fire destroyed majority of the cockpit and fuel system. All the airplane’s primary components were located at the wreckage site. The left wing remained attached to the fuselage and exhibited thermal damage with upward deformation noted about mid-span. The right wing remained attached to the fuselage with impact damage noted to its leading edge skin. Both fuel tanks were breached from impact and thermal damage. Both ailerons were impact-separated and located near the main wreckage. The flaps were thermally damaged and partially separated from the wings. The rudder and vertical stabilizer remained intact with impact damage noted. The left horizontal stabilizer and elevator were displaced aft and partially separated from the fuselage. The right horizontal stabilizer and elevator remained attached to the fuselage with impact damage noted. Rudder control continuity was established from the rudder pedals to the rudder control surface. Aileron and elevator control continuity was established from the cockpit controls through impact separations to the respective flight control surface. The fuselage exhibited impact and thermal damage. The canopy was fragmented and separated from the fuselage. The instrument panel was fragmented. The seats and occupant restraint webbings were thermally destroyed. Two seatbelt receptacles were observed unlatched. The main landing gear was separated from the fuselage with aft deformation noted to the left gear. The engine was separated from the fuselage, and the engine mount was fragmented. The oil sump and exhaust system was fragmented. Crankshaft continuity to the rear gears was established during hand rotation of the attached propeller. Valvetrain continuity was confirmed and compression and suction were attained from all four cylinders. The oil pump suction screen and pressure filter media were clear of debris. The sparkplugs electrodes were intact and exhibited normal wear and coloration when compared to the Champion Check-A-Plug chart. Both magnetos remained attached to the engine and produced spark from their ignition towers during hand rotation of their drive gears. The carburetor was separated from the engine, and its throttle plate was observed in the OPEN position. The ground adjustable, two-blade, composite propeller remained attached to the engine and both propeller blades were fragmented and separated from the hub. The wreckage was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260915203819.s: The pilot of an experimental RV-4 was fatally injured when the aircraft impacted the ground in a steep left bank shortly after departing a private airport. The accident resulted in substantial damage and a postimpact fire, with the investigation finding the engine was running and the throttle was open at impact.

NTSB:20260915203821.n: On September 12, 2026, about 2049 central daylight time, a Beech K35 airplane, N6071E, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Wausau, Wisconsin. The pilot and passenger suffered minor injuries. The flight was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot was conducting a cross-country flight from La Crosse Regional Airport (LSE), La Crosse, Wisconsin, to Wausau Downtown Airport (AUW), Wausau, Wisconsin. The flight departed LSE about 2015. The pilot reported that while flying in the airport traffic pattern for landing at AUW and shortly after he extended the landing gear abeam the runway threshold, he observed a higher-than-normal engine exhaust gas temperature (EGT). According to the pilot, the higher-than-normal engine EGT reminded him to switch fuel tanks. He selected the right fuel tank and advanced the mixture and throttle levers to the full forward position, but the engine did not respond. The pilot stated that he did not turn on the electric fuel boost pump while he attempted to restore engine power. The pilot maneuvered the airplane toward the runway and prepared for a water landing. The airplane impacted water resulting in substantial damage to the fuselage, left wing, left aileron, and engine mount. The pilot and passenger were able to egress from the airplane. The airplane was recovered from the water and secured in a hanger. A postaccident examination revealed that all fuel tank caps were found secure. The right main tank and both auxiliary tanks were full of fuel. The left main tank contained no fuel. The cockpit throttle, mixture, and propeller controls were found in the nearly full forward position. The electric fuel boost pump switch was found turned off. The fuel selector valve was found positioned to the right main fuel tank. The airplane was not equipped with shoulder harnesses, nor was it required to be. According to the pilot, earlier in the day he flew from Langlade County Airport (AIG), Antigo, Wisconsin, to LSE. The airplane departed AIG with full fuel (70 gallons), which was distributed 25 gallons in each main tank and 10 gallons in each auxiliary tank. The pilot did not refuel the airplane at LSE before the flight departed to AUW. The pilot stated that he had the left main fuel tank selected for both flight legs except for when he briefly selected the auxiliary tanks while in cruise flight before switching back to the left tank. In a postaccident interview with a FAA inspector, the pilot’s aviation mechanic stated that he and the pilot discussed the accident, during which the pilot said the loss of engine power was due to his delay in switching fuel tanks and not turning on the electric fuel boost pump.
NTSB:20260915203821.s: The pilot of a Beech K35 experienced engine power loss during the landing pattern at Wausau Downtown Airport due to fuel starvation from the empty left tank and failure to activate the electric boost pump. The pilot attempted a water landing, resulting in substantial damage to the aircraft and minor injuries to both occupants.

NTSB:20260915203828.n: On September 15, 2026 about 1210 Alaska daylight time, a Cessna A185F airplane, N4358Q, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Stony River, Alaska. The pilot and passenger were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 135 air taxi flight. The pilot departed the Aniak Airport (ANI), Aniak, Alaska, about 0910 for a remote hunting camp airstrip near the Fortyseven Creek. About 1020, the pilot reported after landing at the remote airstrip that the wind and turbulence were very strong and he was getting tossed around a lot. He planned to transport two hunters, their moose meat and gear, to the Sleetmute Airport (SLQ), Sleetmute, Alaska, where the hunters were to await further transportation to Anchorage, Alaska. He loaded the first hunter, the hunter’s gear, moose meat and antlers into the airplane. The pilot attempted to load one moose hindquarter into the airplane’s belly pod, but it would not fit and it was left at the airstrip. The passenger and his gear weighed about 300 lbs. The remote airstrip has about 1,600 ft of useable runway. The runway is orientated east to west with a downslope to the east that gets steeper towards the end of the strip. Witnesses report that normally pilots start at the top and have their engine at full throttle by a landmark known as the meat shack or fuel shack. During takeoff on the accident flight, the pilot did not appear to use the entire runway, and it sounded like he delayed application of full power until about 20 to 30 yards past the meat shack. The airplane departed to the east with a left turn to the north. The wind was coming from the south. Witnesses indicated that the wind was so strong they could not hear the sound of the engine of the airplane as it climbed from the runway. Another pilot spotted what he thought was a campfire near the end of the airstrip and flew over to see why someone had started it close to the airstrip. He discovered the accident airplane had impacted terrain and a postcrash fire ensued. Personnel on the ground attempted to reach the accident site but due to thick terrain they could not locate it. A pilot in a Piper PA-18 airplane attempted to guide ground personnel from the air, but due to wind and turbulence was unable to circle the accident site. He elected to circle the wreckage and would advance his throttle over the site to indicate to the personnel on the ground where the wreckage was located. He reported that if he attempted to maneuver over the wreckage the turbulence would have made the airplane uncontrollable. The wreckage was located about 2,400 ft from the airstrip, abeam the departure end on a north heading. A postcrash fire consumed most of the airplane aft of the firewall. A detailed wreckage examination is pending recovery.
NTSB:20260915203828.s: A Part 135 Cessna A185F pilot and passenger were fatally injured when the aircraft impacted terrain shortly after takeoff from a remote airstrip near Stony River, Alaska. Witnesses reported the pilot delayed full power application on a downsloping runway in strong winds, causing the aircraft to strike the ground and burn.

NTSB:20260916203829.n: On September 15, 2026, about 1855 Pacific daylight time, an Airbus Helicopters (formerly Eurocopter) AS-350 B2 helicopter, N358TV, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Chatsworth, California. The pilot, passenger and one person on the ground sustained fatal injuries. The helicopter was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 electronic news gathering flight. According to the operator, the pilot and passenger/news reporter departed Whiteman Airport (WHP) Los Angeles, California, and flew to Chatsworth, California, to gather video footage of a recent fatal traffic accident. ADS-B data showed that the helicopter departed WHP about 1724, proceeded west about nine miles, at an average altitude of about 1,600 ft mean sea level (msl). The helicopter maneuvered in the vicinity of the traffic accident for about one hour and twenty-four minutes. During the last minute of the flight, the helicopter was about 1,700 ft msl or about 800 ft above ground level (agl) and decelerated to about 6 knots ground speed. A four-minute, twenty-one-second-long video recording of the traffic accident was taken by the onboard news reporter. The recording also captured ambient helicopter noise that included sounds from both the main rotor and engine. During most of the recording, the ambient helicopter noise remained consistent with normal operations. During the last twenty-nine seconds of the flight, the recording captured the helicopter noise as it changed frequency, along with intermittent and continuous horns, consistent with the helicopter’s main rotor high rpm, low rotor rpm and other aural advisories. About 1855, ADS-B data showed that the helicopter began a rapid descent while turning right. The last ADS-B data point captured the helicopter at a high rate of descent, about 38 knots groundspeed directly above the accident site. Multiple security video cameras from nearby buildings recorded the helicopter as it descended at a high rate and impacted a metal storage container. A postaccident fire quickly ensued. Postaccident field examination revealed the helicopter came to rest partially on its right side abeam the metal container. A debris field extended about 30 ft around the main wreckage. All major components remained attached to the fuselage or remained within the small debris area. The fuselage, in its entirety, was mostly reduced to ash and thermally damaged metal. The tailboom separated but remained next to the fuselage. Both main and tail rotor assemblies remained attached at their respective mounting assemblies. The helicopter was relocated to a secure facility for further examination.
NTSB:20260916203829.s: An Airbus AS-350 B2 helicopter operating a Part 91 news gathering flight crashed near Chatsworth, California, killing the pilot, passenger, and one person on the ground. The accident occurred during a low-speed hover when the helicopter entered a rapid descent and impacted a metal storage container, likely triggered by rotor RPM anomalies.

NTSB:20260916203834.n: The pilot of the business jet reported that during an instrument approach to runway 28, while crossing the initial approach fix, he received the automated weather observation system (AWOS) wind report, which stated the wind was from 190° at 9 knots. He flew the instrument approach uneventfully at reference speed plus 20 knots until landing was assured and then reduced engine power. After touchdown, the airplane drifted right and the pilot corrected back toward centerline; however, the airplane then turned sharply left and exited the left side of the runway, striking a windsock and taxi light before coming to rest upright on a grass area. The airplane's right wing and fuselage were substantially damaged during the accident sequence. The pilot reported that there were no preimpact mechanical malfunctions with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation. Review of recorded weather data revealed that 25 minutes prior to the accident, the wind was from 170° at 6 knots. The recorded wind 5 minutes before the accident was from 190° at 16 knots, gusting to 26 knots. Given this information, it is likely that the pilot had outdated wind information was not aware of the severity of the left crosswind, which contributed to his loss of directional control while landing.
NTSB:20260916203834.s: The business jet pilot lost directional control during landing on runway 28 after relying on outdated AWOS wind data that underestimated a severe left crosswind. The aircraft exited the runway left, striking a windsock and taxi light, causing substantial damage to the right wing and fuselage.

NTSB:20260917203837.n: On September 17, 2026, about 0720 eastern daylight time, a Weatherly Aviation Company Inc. 602B, N20003, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Lynchburg, South Carolina. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 137 aerial application flight. According to a family member, the pilot departed a private airstrip in Woodrow, South Carolina and flew to a private airstrip in Oswego, South Carolina. The airplane was loaded with about 20 gallons of herbicide, which was to be applied on a nearby corn field. The flight was planned to take about 30 to 45 minutes. According to the landowner, he received a phone call from a family member of the pilot asking if the pilot had completed the job. The landowner subsequently saw smoke in the vicinity of the corn field and found the airplane inverted and on fire. The accident site was located about 10 miles east of the departure location. The airplane impacted the ground on magnetic heading of 134o, at an elevation of 154 ft mean sea level (msl). The debris field measured 300 ft by 180 ft with all major components of the airplane located within the debris field. The right wing was impact separated and located 96 ft from the initial ground impact with the right main landing gear assembly still attached. The leading edge of the right wing was crushed aft with engine oil on the wing surface. The fuselage, left wing, and empennage came to rest on a magnetic heading of 255o. The fuselage was partially consumed by a postaccident fire from the cockpit forward. The left wing was partially attached to the fuselage with thermal damage at the wing root and the leading edge crushed aft. The empennage remained attached to the fuselage with the left elevator crushed. The rudder was impact separated and was found near the engine about 20 ft from the fuselage. The rudder exhibited thermal damage to the lower rudder cap. The engine, engine mount, and firewall were separated and came to rest about 20 ft from the fuselage. Engine cylinder Nos. 3, 4, and 5 exhibited impact damage to the cylinder head assemblies. The No. 2-cylinder head was fractured. It did not display impact damage and was found within the debris field. The accessory section of the engine, the firewall, and engine mount exhibited thermal damage. The wreckage was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260917203837.s: A Weatherly Aviation 602B pilot conducting an aerial application flight was fatally injured when the aircraft impacted the ground inverted and caught fire near Lynchburg, South Carolina. The accident occurred while the pilot was applying herbicide over a cornfield, resulting in substantial damage to the aircraft and a post-accident fire.

NTSB:20260917203838.n: On September 16, 2026, about 1905 eastern daylight time, a Cessna 172M airplane, N9909Q, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Hanover, Indiana. The pilot and passenger sustained minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot reported that the purpose of the flight was to fly with a friend to and from Lee Bottom Airport. The pilot stated that she was familiar with the airport's grass runway and previously operated there during flight training. After landing at Lee Bottom, the pilot taxied back for departure from runway 18. During the initial takeoff the pilot noted that the airplane was not performing as expected and discontinued the takeoff. The pilot taxied back and initiated a second takeoff attempt using 10° flaps. The pilot reported that, during the second takeoff, the airplane became airborne and remained in ground effect to gain airspeed, and then the pilot established a climb. As the airplane approached trees beyond the departure end of the runway, the pilot reported that the trees appeared to be getting closer and attempted to clear them. The pilot then observed a decrease in airspeed and lowered the nose. The airplane subsequently contacted the tops of trees, continued through the trees, impacted a residence, and then impacted terrain. The airplane came to rest inverted. There were no injuries reported on ground. The pilot and passenger exited the airplane after the accident with minor injuries. The fuselage and wings sustained substantial damage and the airplane was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260917203838.s: A Cessna 172M pilot and passenger sustained minor injuries when the aircraft struck trees and a residence during departure from Lee Bottom Airport. The pilot reported the airplane lost airspeed while attempting to clear obstacles after a second takeoff attempt with 10° flaps, resulting in substantial damage.

NTSB:20260917203839.n: On September 7, 2026, about 1059 central daylight time, a Cessna 172N airplane, N734NM, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Panama City, Florida. The student pilot and flight instructor were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight. The flight instructor reported that this was his second flight of the day in the accident airplane, and that there were no abnormalities experienced during the first flight. Prior to the accident flight, a preflight inspection and engine run-up were completed with no indication of any abnormalities. A normal takeoff was accomplished with the airplane accelerating normally to rotation speed. During initial climb, about 300 ft above ground level, both pilots observed a loss of engine power, despite the throttle and mixture controls being in the full forward position. The flight instructor continued that there was no smoke, vibration, or "catastrophic engine noise" coincident with the loss of power. The flight instructor took control of the airplane and executed an emergency forced landing, straight ahead, onto airport property. During the forced landing, the airplane's right wing struck a runway approach light which resulted in substantial damage. The airplane was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260917203839.s: A student pilot and flight instructor in a Cessna 172N experienced sudden engine power loss at 300 feet AGL during initial climb. The instructor executed a forced landing onto airport property, where the right wing struck an approach light, causing substantial damage.

NTSB:20260918203844.n: On September 17, 2026, about 1930 Alaska daylight time, a Piper PA-18-150 airplane, N9128D, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Northway, Alaska. The pilot and passenger were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 135 on-demand air taxi flight. According to company employees, packers, guides, and hunters were at a moose camp along the Snag Creek known as the “Snag strip.” The purpose of the flight was to transport one of the packers to another moose camp, located about 10 miles east of their position. The employees observed the pilot perform a preflight inspection and load the packer and his backpack into the airplane. They then observed the pilot taxi and takeoff. After the airplane became airborne, the employees turned away and did not observe anything unusual. Shortly thereafter, they heard sounds described as metal popping and observed the airplane on the ground on the opposite side of the creek. The airplane came to rest on a north heading, about 750 ft from the dirt airstrip at an elevation of 3,280 ft. They described the weather as a good flying day with light winds. An investigator from the NTSB Alaska Regional office conducted an on-scene examination of the wreckage. All major components of the airplane remained attached and were accounted for at the accident site. The initial observed impact point was a large bush a few feet in front of the wreckage, where a partially severed branch about 5 ft. above the ground was observed. An upper portion of the bush contained cut marks, while the remainder of the bush was largely undamaged. The airplane subsequently impacted the gravel riverbed in a nose-low attitude near the shoreline, rotated, and came to rest facing opposite the general direction of travel. Flight control continuity was confirmed from the cockpit controls to the respective flight control surfaces. The leading edges were crushed inward. The left and right wing vortex generators were located in the riverbed in a line that paralleled the wings on the ground in front of the airplane. The wing flaps were extended to the second notch. The vertical and horizontal stabilizers appeared undamaged, and the rudder and elevators remained attached. The fuselage was separated forward of the control stick. The instrument panel and the firewall were separated from the fuselage. No control stick was installed in the backseat. The fuel selector was on the LEFT fuel tank. The fuel tanks were breached during the accident sequence. The airplane was recovered to a secure facility for further examination. The flaps had been modified with an STC, they moved freely and with no biding or anomalies noted. The stabilizer trim jackscrew was in a partial nose down trim setting. The carburetor was impact separated from the engine, but the control cables remained attached. Fuel from the header tank and the aft header tank were drained and captured, it was blue and consistent with 100LL. The fuel was tested for the presence of water and was negative. A light borescope inspection was performed on all cylinders, normal combustion deposits were observed, no anomalies were noted. The engine was rotated by hand, and thumb compression was observed on all cylinders. Both magnetos remained attached to the engine, they were removed and rotated by hand. The left magneto produced spark when rotated, the right magneto did not. Further examination of the right magneto revealed fractured aluminum around its attach flange consistent with impact damage. The oil screen was removed and was clean and unobstructed. Oil was observed in the sump, it was light golden brown in color. The condition of all spark plugs was consistent with normal when compared to the Champion Aviation Check-A-Plug chart. The propeller remained attached to the crankshaft propeller flange. Both blades exhibited chordwise scoring and leading edge nicks and gouges. A Garmin Aera was recovered from and sent to the NTSB Recorders Laboratory for download.
NTSB:20260918203844.s: A Piper PA-18-150 operating a Part 135 air taxi flight crashed shortly after takeoff near Northway, Alaska, killing the pilot and passenger. Witnesses heard metal popping before the aircraft impacted a bush and riverbed, with investigators finding the right magneto fractured by impact and the stabilizer trim set nose-down.

NTSB:20260921203845.n: On September 20, 2026, at 1356 Pacific daylight time, an Airbus AS332 L1 Super Puma, N332N, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Yosemite Valley, California. The two pilots were fatally injured. The helicopter was operated as a public use firefighting flight. Earlier in the day, the pilots conducted a 2.9 hour firefighting flight where they dropped water from an 800-gallon Nomad bucket that was attached to a 200 ft longline. After finishing the helicopter’s fuel cycle and completing over 25 drops, they returned back to their helibase. During that flight, they had problems with the water bucket and upon landing, the mechanics tightened the bucket’s air pressure regulator and pressure checked the system. Shortly thereafter, they received a request to perform water drops on fires near helispot H-5, using Ostrander Lake as the dip site. A review of FAA ADS-B data, Spidertracks data, and firefighter’s cell phone videos revealed that the helicopter made three dips at the lake and the accident occurred during the helicopter’s third drop (see figure 1). Figure 1: ADS-B data showing the helicopter's dip and drop site The helicopter departed the helibase about 1328 and continued toward the requested drop area, consistent with the flight crew assessing the drop site before loading water in the bucket. The pilots then flew to the dip site and coordinated with two other helicopters that were operating out of the site. After filling the bucket with a load of water that was less than full, the pilots flew about 2.25 nautical miles (nm) to drop area and then made a trailing drop at about 1345 before returning to the dip site (see figure 2). Figure 2: ADS-B data showing the flight path before the first drop as well as photos from the drop showing the bucket The pilots again filled the bucket and flew to the drop site. The helicopter approached the area about 8,690 ft mean sea level (msl) and gradually descended for a concentrated, or spot, drop on a dead tree (snag). The ground crew provided a strobe light to help aid the pilots in identifying the desired drop location. The drop occurred about 1350:50, with the bucket remaining just above the approximately 80- to 125-ft tree canopy (see figure 2). Figure 3: ADS-B data showing the flight path before the second drop as well as photos from the drop showing the bucket The helicopter returned to the dip site, the pilots filled the bucket and continued back to the drop area. The helicopter’s groundspeed generally decreased as the descent rate increased. The firefighting ground crew reported that the water was dropped in the same location as drop 2, which according to the ground crew, was the desired location. The water drop began about 1356:28 and the bucket was empty about 3 seconds later, which was followed by the helicopter yawing to the left about 1 second later (see figure 4 and 5). At 1356:37, the helicopter’s ground speed was 4 kts and the descent rate was about 1,344 feet per minute (fpm). Figure 4: ADS-B data showing the flight path before the third drop as well as photos from the drop showing the bucket Figure 5: Descent before impact with ground speed and descent rate from ADS-B The bucket appeared to drop almost vertically and then contacted the ground about 1356:38. The cargo hook was released about one second later which allowed the longline to fall and the helicopter appeared to move forward about 1356:40 (see figures 6 and 7). The helicopter contacted trees about 1356:43, followed by the sound of impact about one second later. Figure 6: Video compilation showing bucket vertically descending Figure 7: Excerpt of video showing the hook release for the bucket and bucket position in wreckage A preliminary review was conducted on the audio from some of the videos taken. The video soundtrack was used to estimate main rotor speed (NR) and engine gas-generator speed (Ng) during the accident sequence. A comparison of the frequencies recorded and those known of the helicopter’s operation indicated that NR was about 102% at 13:56:13 and about 101% near the time of the water drop. Ng was estimated at about 90% before the water drop, increased to 96.9% shortly afterward, and subsequently increased to about 101.2%. Near the end of the sequence, NR was estimated at about 96%. The soundtrack analysis also identified the acoustic event associated with blade impact at about 13:56:42. The accident site was located in the Yosemite National Park at an elevation of about 8,150 ft mean sea level (msl). The main wreckage was positioned on sloping terrain about 500 ft downslope from the relatively flat area that comprised helispot H-5. The surrounding terrain was densely forested with tall fir trees. The tree canopy was about 100 to 150 ft above ground level (agl), depending on the slope of the terrain. There were several trees in the immediate area of the wreckage that were severed consistent with the helicopter’s impact into the canopy. The main wreckage came to rest on its left side with the nose oriented upslope. A majority of the helicopter was consumed by postimpact fire. The cockpit and instrument panel were extensively fire damaged, and no meaningful data could be obtained from most of the cockpit gauges. The bucket was located about 90 ft west-northwest from the main wreckage adjacent to an area of dirt that had the appearance of being disrupted from a water drop (see figure 8). The cargo hook was found in the locked position, consistent with a normal electronic release, rather than use of the manual release. Figure 8: Main wreckage in reference to bucket The cockpit voice recorder was retained and downloaded. The wreckage is being recovered pending the fire danger in the area and is planned to be examined at a future date.
NTSB:20260921203845.s: Two pilots were fatally injured when an Airbus AS332 L1 Super Puma crashed near Yosemite Valley during a firefighting water drop. The accident occurred after the third drop when the helicopter yawed left, descended rapidly, and impacted trees following the bucket's release.

NTSB:20260921203846.n: On September 18, 2026, at 1604 eastern daylight time, an Aerospatiale SA315B helicopter, N238HA was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Workmore, Georgia. The pilot was not injured. The helicopter was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 137 aerial application flight. According to the pilot, he arrived at a field to conduct an agricultural aerial application. He landed the helicopter on the tanker truck and the helicopter was refilled with 145 gallons of product. The pilot stated that at the time of takeoff, all engine temperatures were normal. The helicopter lifted off the truck and began to make a sound that he described as a piece of plastic or paper on a main rotor blade. The pilot attempted to reach an suitable area for landing but had only attained an altitude of about 40 feet above ground level and was losing lift. The pilot then "pulled the collective to correct lift loss" but the helicopter did not respond as expected. When he realized he was not going to make his landing area, he "pulled all of the cyclic" to slow the descent rate but the helicopter did not respond. The helicopter landed hard 300 feet from the tanker truck. The tail rotor impacted the ground and main rotor blades severed the tail rotor from the tail boom. A small postaccident fire ensued behind the helicopter around the tail boom area. The helicopter sustained substantial damage to the tail rotor, the tail boom, fuselage and the main rotor blades. The helicopter was recovered and retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260921203846.s: During a Part 137 aerial application takeoff, an Aerospatiale SA315B helicopter suffered lift loss and unresponsive controls at 40 feet AGL. The pilot executed a hard landing 300 feet from the tanker truck, causing substantial damage to the tail rotor, boom, and main blades, followed by a small postaccident fire.

NTSB:20260921203847.n: On September 19, 2026, at 1045 eastern daylight time, a Cirrus SR-20, N189WM, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Ashville, North Carolina. The flight instructor and the student pilot received minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight. The flight instructor reported that, during the pre-takeoff run-up, while checking the magnetos, the engine rpm dropped by 100 on the right and 150 on the left. Unable to resolve the discrepancy, they taxied back and troubleshot the issue further with the chief flight instructor. The flight instructor was informed that the anomaly was discovered on previous flights and that the mixture needed to be precisely leaned for density altitude. They were departing from Asheville Regional Airport (AVL) Asheville, North Carolina, which had a field elevation of 2,163 ft. After receiving the information, the pilot leaned the fuel mixture, and the magneto check was within limits. No further anomalies were observed. After taxi out, while holding short of the takeoff runway, the instructor performed another engine run-up and checked the magnetos, which yielded normal results. During the takeoff roll, all gauges and indications were reading normal, and the engine was performing normally during the takeoff roll and climb out. During the later stages of the climb, the instructor noticed that the engine cylinder head temperatures (CHTs) were reading a little high, so he enriched the mixture to keep the CHT below 400°. About 10 seconds after adding mixture, while at an altitude of about 3,000 ft, mean sea level the engine lost all power. The instructor took over the controls, turned back toward the airport, and declared an emergency. His attempts to restart the engine were unsuccessful and he pitched for best glide speed. During the descent, they were still over mountainous terrain at 2,000 ft above ground level and the flight instructor determined it was too risky to activate the Cirrus Airframe Parachute System (CAPS) so he aimed towards the first open field and intended to pull the CAPS as soon as they arrived over the field or at 800 ft agl, “whichever came first.” Once over the field, the instructor activated the CAPS; the parachute deployed and the airplane descended and settled onto the field. During the landing, the nose gear collapsed, and the engine compartment and airframe forward of the cockpit were substantially damaged. The wreckage was recovered and retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260921203847.s: A flight instructor and student in a Cirrus SR-20 experienced total engine power loss at 3,000 feet MSL shortly after enriching the mixture to manage high cylinder head temperatures. The instructor activated the Airframe Parachute System over a field, resulting in substantial damage when the nose gear collapsed upon landing.

NTSB:20260921203848.n: On September 18, 2026, about 1426 eastern daylight time, a Schempp-Hirth Ventus-2B glider, N61XC, and a Schleicher ASW-24 glider, N94CG, collided in flight near Edinburg, New York. The pilot of the Schempp-Hirth was fatally injured and the glider was destroyed. The pilot of the Schleicher was not injured and the glider was substantially damaged. The gliders were operated as Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flights. The pilot of the Schleicher glider stated that there were four gliders flying in a thermal. They were flying at an altitude of about 5,000 ft mean sea level when the Schempp-Hirth glider descended from above and its left wing contacted the nose section of his glider. He further stated that he retained controllability of the glider, so he circled and landed at Plateau Sky Ranch Airport (1F2), Edinburg, New York. During the turn to circle the airport, the pilot of the Schleicher glider saw the left wing of the Schempp-Hirth fracture off before the glider fell to the ground. The Schempp-Hirth glider came to rest in a wooded area about 5 miles north of 1F2. The right wing and empennage were located near the impact crater. The glider was fractured into several pieces. The left wing was not located. Flight track data recovered from recording devices onboard both gliders were downloaded for further examination. NTSB:20260921203848.s: Two glider pilots collided while circling a thermal at 5,000 feet near Edinburg, New York. The Schempp-Hirth descended from above, striking the Schleicher's nose, which caused the Schempp-Hirth to break apart and crash, killing its pilot, while the Schleicher pilot landed safely.

NTSB:20260921203850.n: On September 18, 2026, at 1018 eastern daylight time, a Bell 206B-III, N50141, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Creswell, North Carolina. The pilot was not injured. The helicopter was being operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 137 aerial application flight. According to the pilot, the helicopter was 40-50 ft above the ground on approach to land when he heard a "whooshing" noise and noticed the engine lost partial power and main rotor RPM had begun to decay. Subsequently, the helicopter landed hard, which resulted in substantial damage to the tail boom. The engine continued to operate after landing until it was shut down normally by the pilot. The helicopter was recovered to a secure location for further examination.
NTSB:20260921203850.s: During a Part 137 aerial application approach, the pilot of a Bell 206B-III reported partial engine power loss and decaying main rotor RPM at 40–50 feet. The helicopter subsequently landed hard, causing substantial damage to the tail boom, though the pilot was uninjured.

NTSB:20260922203852.n: According to the pilot of the experimental amateur-built airplane, on the final leg of a cross-country flight he detected an odor, and as the odor intensified, he also noticed an increase in heat. The pilot decided to divert to the nearest airport and then observed a reduction in engine power and oil droplets on his windscreen. While he searched for a suitable landing site he observed fluctuating oil pressure, followed by an audible oil pressure warning tone. The pilot initiated off-airport landing to a field. The airplane subsequently impacted a fence and sustained substantial damage to the fuselage and both wings. During a post-accident examination of the engine the turbocharger down pipe exhaust clamp bolt was missing, and the exhaust down pipe had disconnected. Additionally, the turbocharger oil return line exhibited thermal damage and was saturated with engine oil. Given these findings, it is likely that the release of hot exhaust gases prevented the turbocharger's waste gate from functioning normally and resulted in the partial loss of engine power observed by the pilot. The thermal damage to the oil return line likely resulted in the fluctuating engine oil pressure and subsequent loss of oil.
NTSB:20260922203852.s: The pilot of an experimental amateur-built airplane diverted and made an off-airport landing after detecting heat, oil loss, and power reduction caused by a disconnected turbocharger exhaust pipe. The resulting hot exhaust gases likely disabled the waste gate and damaged the oil return line, leading to a fence impact and substantial damage.

NTSB:20260922203853.n: On September 20, 2026 about 2314 central daylight time, a Piper PA-28-140 airplane, N224BB, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Junction, Texas. The pilot and passenger were seriously injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to the pilot, he completed a preflight inspection and engine run-up of the airplane and found no anomalies. He verified all gauges were in the green and departed the Kimble County Airport (JCT) at about 2312L. At about 600 ft above the ground the engine rpm decreased from 2560 rpm to 1,100 rpm. The pilot increased the mixture control to the full rich position, moved the engine throttle to full power and engaged the engine starter but the engine remained at 1,100 rpm. When he engaged the engine starter, he determined the engine was still running. He trimmed the airplane for best glide and made a force landing to a heavily treed area. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage and wings. A detailed wreckage examination is pending.
NTSB:20260922203853.s: The pilot and passenger of a Piper PA-28-140 were seriously injured when the engine RPM dropped to 1,100 at 600 feet AGL shortly after departure from Kimble County Airport. Despite attempts to restore power, the pilot executed a forced landing into a treed area, causing substantial damage to the fuselage and wings.

NTSB:20260924203863.n: On September 23, 2026, about 1711 Pacific daylight time, a Cessna 172B, N44P, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Royal City, Washington. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to the pilot’s family, he departed from a private airstrip on his property at about 1630. Shortly thereafter, a worker at a farm located near B & G Farms Airport (4WA0), Royal City, Washington, saw the airplane land on runway 7. The worker periodically turned his attention to the airplane and saw it back-taxi to the approach end of runway 7 and stand with the engine running for about 20 minutes. The witness saw the airplane taxi in one or two circles before it lined up with runway 7 and began its departure roll. The airplane’s takeoff appeared normal until it rotated into a nose high pitch attitude as it passed a building located alongside the runway. The airplane began to climb steeply, yawed left, and overflew a road and residence. The airplane then rolled to the left, its nose dropped, and it subsequently impacted a farm field about 450 ft north of the runway. (See figure.) The witness stated he could hear the airplane’s engine running during the entire flight without any irregularities or changes in tone. Figure: A depiction of airplane’s flight path, as described by the witness. The airplane came to rest inverted on an approximate magnetic heading of 070°. The first identified point of impact was a divot in soft mud that contained fragments of the landing and taxi light lens from the left wing. The left wing was crushed aft outboard of the lift strut, and mud had adhered to the leading edge. The right wing leading edge was crushed aft. Both flaps appeared to be in the retracted position. The engine, engine mount, and firewall were displaced aft. The pilot’s seat was separated from the seat rails and the seat pins were bent. The seat rails were partially separated from the floor, and one seat rail was bent around the seat base roller assembly. The wreckage was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260924203863.s: A Cessna 172B pilot was fatally injured when the aircraft impacted a field shortly after departing runway 7 at B & G Farms Airport. The witness reported the plane climbed steeply, yawed left, and rolled left before impact, with the engine running normally throughout the flight.

NTSB:20260924203864.n: On September 23, 2026, about 1755 central daylight time, an experimental Magni M16 gyroplane, N109MG, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Annapolis, Missouri. The pilot and passenger were both fatally injured. The gyroplane was operated under the provisions of Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 as a personal flight. First responders located the gyroplane and reported it had collided with power lines and impacted terrain. A power outage in the area was also reported. FAA inspectors responded to the accident scene and examined the wreckage. The debris field, which began with separated sections of the pusher propeller, was about 100 yards in length. Portions of the horizontal stabilizer and rudder system were located about midway through the debris field. A ground scar consistent with ground collision was found about 10 to 15 yards north of the main wreckage, surrounded by fragments of windscreen, airframe pieces, and rotor blades. The gyroplane came to rest on its left side, and cyclic and rudder control continuity appeared to be continuous. Fuel was observed in the fuel tank. A power line was entangled in the main wreckage. The gyroplane was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260924203864.s: On September 23, 2026, a pilot and passenger were fatally injured when their experimental Magni M16 gyroplane, N109MG, collided with power lines and impacted terrain near Annapolis, Missouri. The accident caused substantial damage to the aircraft, including a separated pusher propeller and entangled power lines, during a personal flight.

NTSB:20260924203867.n: On September 24, 2026, about 0945 Pacific daylight time, an Aeronca 7AC, N12DF, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Hesperia, California. The flight instructor and passenger were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to the operator of the airplane, the pilot had rented the airplane and departed from Apple Valley Airport (APV), Apple Valley, California, on the day of the accident flight. A destination was not offered by the pilot, just a basic query as to where to go for breakfast. The accident was witnessed by multiple people within the vicinity of the accident site. One witness stated that due to construction equipment, they could not hear the airplane, however, they noticed a small airplane flying in the area. They recalled that the tail appeared lower than the wings with the tail moving laterally from right to left before the airplane rolled over and he was able to see the belly of the airplane. The airplane’s nose was pointed down and then he saw the airplane descend toward terrain. Examination of the accident site revealed that the airplane impacted terrain about 1.5 miles southwest of Hesperia Airport (L26), Hesperia, California. The airplane came to rest in a nose down attitude, in open desert terrain on a heading of about 160° magnetic, at an elevation of 3,584 ft mean seal level (msl). There was no visible ground scar observed surrounding the wreckage. The propeller assembly and propeller blades remained attached to the engine and the engine was pushed aft toward the firewall. The undercarriage of the cockpit was crushed forward toward the engine, with the empennage and tail at an almost 90° degree angle. Both wings remained attached to the fuselage and had sustained leading edge crush damage throughout. The airplane was recovered to a secure facility for further examination.
NTSB:20260924203867.s: A flight instructor and passenger were fatally injured when their rented Aeronca 7AC, N12DF, impacted terrain near Hesperia, California, during a Part 91 personal flight. Witnesses observed the aircraft flying with a low tail and lateral movement before rolling over and descending nose-down into open desert.

NTSB:20260924203873.n: On September 24, 2026, about 0958 mountain daylight time, an experimental amateur-built Zenith CH750 STOL airplane, N750WZ, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Silver Creek, Nevada. The pilot was not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot reported that shortly after he reached his planned altitude he pulled the throttle back to level off. He noticed that he had lost the indications for the No. 1 cylinder head temperature and exhaust gas temperature. Subsequently, the engine started to run rough, and the pilot initiated a turn back to his departure airport. After the pilot made a radio call he lost all power and the propeller seized. The pilot initiated a forced landing on a highway and subsequently opted to land in a field to avoid vehicular traffic. During the landing roll the nose landing gear impacted an embankment and the airplane pitched up onto its nose, which resulted in substantial damage to the fuselage. The pilot reported that at the time of the accident the engine had accrued about 540 hours of operation and 15 hours since the last inspection, which was completed on August 25, 2026. The airplane was recovered to a secure location for further examination.
NTSB:20260924203873.s: The pilot of an experimental Zenith CH750 STOL experienced engine roughness and power loss shortly after reaching planned altitude, forcing a landing in a field. The nose gear struck an embankment during the roll, pitching the aircraft up and causing substantial fuselage damage.

NTSB:20260926203879.n: On September 26, 2026, about 1120 eastern daylight time, an Aero Commander 112, N1102J, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Chatsworth, Georgia. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to the pilot’s wife, the purpose of the flight was to reposition the airplane from Martin Campbell Field (1A3), Copperhill, Tennessee, to Dalton Municipal Airport (DNN), Dalton, Georgia. She stated that she dropped the pilot off at 1A3 on the morning of the accident about 0930 so that he could pick up the airplane from maintenance. She recalled that the pilot had taken the airplane for maintenance after the pilot heard an audible warning noise related to the left main landing gear after turning on the airplane electrical power. She stated that the mechanic believed it was a switch, so he sprayed the switch with a water displacing chemical and then cycled the landing gear several times. On the morning before the flight, the mechanic had planned to cycle the landing gear one last time before the pilot took the airplane to DNN. According to ADS-B data provided by the FAA, the airplane departed from 1A3 at 1056 and flew toward the south. The airplane then turned toward the west at 1103 and continue toward DNN. The airplane’s final ADS-B observed position was recorded at 1110, with the airplane at an altitude of 4,600 ft mean sea level (msl) and located about 11 miles east of DNN. The accident site was located in a small hay field about 1 mile southeast of DNN, and there were no known witnesses to the accident. The wreckage was examined at the accident site. The right fuel tank was breached, and the fuel selector was observed in between the right fuel tank and off positions. Air was blown through the right fuel line at the wing root, through the fuel selector to the firewall with no blockages observed. Fuel was present at the firewall when air was applied to the right fuel system line. The fuel strainer was impact-separated from the airplane. Fuel was found within the fuel injector unit. The fuel manifold did not contain any debris and the fuel lines to the fuel injectors were secure. The fuel injectors were unobstructed. The engine-driven fuel pump, oil filter, and fuel injector unit were impact-separated from the engine. The engine’s crankshaft was rotated by hand when force was applied to the crankshaft flange. Thumb compression and suction were observed on all four cylinders, valve action movement was observed, and continuity of the crankshaft to the camshaft was observed throughout the engine. The engine cylinders were examined with a lighted borescope and no anomalies were observed. No evidence of any preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures of the engine were observed. The airplane was equipped with a two-blade, controllable-pitch propeller. One propeller blade remained straight and was undamaged. The second blade was bent aft about 8 inches from the tip. Video footage obtained from first responders showed that fuel was visibly leaking steadily from the right fuel tank when they arrived at the accident site. According to the mechanic who had performed the most recent maintenance of the airplane, the airplane had consistently had small problems since the pilot purchased it. Most recently, the pilot was having a problem starting the engine. The mechanic flow-tested the fuel injector nozzles and found that they were not flowing evenly, so he replaced them with new nozzles. During the fuel nozzle troubleshooting, the mechanic removed a piece of debris, similar to silicone, from the fuel injector line. The pilot also had a problem starting the engine on a recent flight that was attributed to the Bendix drive on the starter not engaging, so he replaced the starter. Most recently, and in the days prior to the accident flight, the pilot reported to him that when he turned on electrical power, he immediately saw and heard the left main landing gear unlocked indication and horn. The mechanic attributed it to a sticking switch, so he sprayed it with a water displacing spray and cycled the gear several times. He then left the airplane on jacks and cycled the gear one last time on morning of the accident flight. The mechanic added that during the engine runup, he radioed to the pilot that if he had a left gear unlocked indication during the flight, it was likely just that switch, and that he should not be concerned. The mechanic provided a fuel receipt that showed the pilot had obtained 35.6 gallons of 100LL the day prior to the flight. Audio of the DNN common traffic advisory frequency was obtained from a security camera mounted in the lobby of the airport that also captured radio traffic. The audio included radio calls from the accident pilot, and no distress calls could be heard. Flight logbooks for the pilot were reviewed, but no entries were made after June 21, 2026. The pilot’s wife stated that the pilot flew several times after the last logbook entry date. At the time of the last logbook entry, the pilot recorded a total of 125.7 hours. He had accumulated a total of 14.9 hours in the accident airplane as of the last recorded logbook entry. The pilot received his complex airplane endorsement on July 15, 2025. The wreckage was recovered and retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260926203879.s: The pilot of an Aero Commander 112 was fatally injured when the aircraft crashed near Dalton, Georgia, during a personal flight. The investigation found no preimpact engine failure, but noted a breached right fuel tank with the selector between positions and a history of unresolved fuel and landing gear issues.

NTSB:20260927203880.n: On September 27, 2026, about 1608 central daylight time, an experimental PA-18 Replica airplane, N43LK, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Buffalo, Minnesota. The pilot was fatally injured, and the pilot-rated passenger was seriously injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. A witness reported that the airplane took off from runway 18 and appeared to be climbing at a steep angle. He described the engine sound as “loud.” Shortly afterward, the airplane rolled off and entered a steep descent before impacting the ground. Figure 1 – Airplane at accident site. Initial ground impressions were consistent with a nose-down impact at the north edge of taxiway A1. The airplane came to rest at the taxiway A1 hold short line which was about 27 ft southwest from the initial impact and oriented on a southeast heading. The wings were dislocated and resting in position relative to the fuselage. Both wings exhibited leading edge crushing damage along the entire span. The engine was displaced upward relative to the fuselage, and the cockpit area was compromised. The aft fuselage was oriented upward with the empennage intact. The flight control surfaces remained attached to the airframe. The control cables were secured to the respective control surfaces. They were continuous to the wing roots, for the ailerons and flaps, and to the cockpit area for the elevators and rudder. Flight control cable separations were retained for further examination. FAA records revealed that the airplane was issued an experimental special airworthiness certificate on June 25, 2026. The records listed no flight time (0.0 hours) for the airplane as a newly constructed aircraft when the certificate was issued. Current flight time for the airplane was not available at the time of accident. FAA records also revealed that the pilot was issued a private pilot certificate on August 12, 2026. At that time, he had logged 75.8 hours total flight time with 17.2 hours of pilot-in-command and 5.2 hours of tailwheel airplane flight time. His logbook contained a tailwheel airplane endorsement. No flight time was logged subsequent to the issuance of his private pilot certificate.
NTSB:20260927203880.s: The pilot of an experimental PA-18 Replica, N43LK, was fatally injured when the aircraft crashed shortly after takeoff from runway 18 near Buffalo, Minnesota. A witness reported the plane climbed steeply with a loud engine sound before rolling off and entering a steep descent, resulting in substantial damage.

NTSB:20260928203884.n: On September 27, 2026, about 1202 Pacific daylight time, an experimental amateur-built Bearhawk Patrol, N240BP, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Cottage Grove, Oregon. The pilot sustained serious injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot reported that, during the initial climb at an altitude of approximately 2,300 ft mean sea level (msl), he reduced the propeller speed from 2,650 rpm to 2,500 rpm. Immediately thereafter, he thought the engine had an uncontained failure and components had struck the windscreen, which obstructed his forward visibility. Using his view through the left side window, the pilot maneuvered toward a suitable off-airport landing area. During the descent, the stall warning horn activated, and the pilot lowered the airplane's nose and continued the approach to a field. The airplane subsequently touched down on uneven grassy terrain and came to rest upright. Post accident examination of the airplane revealed that the fuselage was substantially damaged. The engine cowling was displaced upward and aft, onto the windscreen. No visible holes were observed within the engine crankcase. The 2 bladed constant speed propeller remained attached to the engine crankshaft; however, one of the two blades was separated from the propeller hub and was not located at the accident site. The airplane was recovered to a secure location for further examination.
NTSB:20260928203884.s: The pilot of an experimental Bearhawk Patrol, N240BP, sustained serious injuries when the aircraft was substantially damaged during initial climb near Cottage Grove, Oregon. The pilot reported an apparent uncontained engine failure that displaced the cowling onto the windscreen and separated a propeller blade, forcing an off-airport landing.

NTSB:20260929203889.n: On September 27, 2026, about 1333 central daylight time, a Beech A33 airplane, N1288Z, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near East Troy, Wisconsin. The pilot and three passengers sustained minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to the pilot, the airplane had a sudden total loss of engine power after a low approach. He stated that during the climb out from the low approach at the East Troy Municipal Airport (57C), the engine suddenly stopped but did not seize or show any abnormalities before the loss of power. The pilot attempted to restart the engine; however, the engine did not respond. The pilot chose an open agricultural field off to the right and conducted and forced landing. During the forced landing, the airplane impacted agricultural vegetation and impact terrain which resulted in substantial damage to both wings, the fuselage, and the empennage. The airplane was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260929203889.s: The pilot of a Beech A33 conducting a Part 91 flight reported a sudden total engine power loss during climbout after a low approach at East Troy Municipal Airport. The pilot executed a forced landing in an agricultural field, resulting in substantial damage to the aircraft and minor injuries to all four occupants.

NTSB:20260929203890.n: On September 27, 2026, about 1720 central daylight time, a Haberman Habercraft airplane, N10516, was substantially damaged during an accident near Pelican Rapids, Minnesota. The pilot sustained a minor injury. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot reported that before the flight the 12-gallon fuselage fuel tank contained about 8.5 gallons of fuel and that the cork-and-wire fuel indicator gauge installed in the fuel tank cap was about 5.5 inches above an empty indication. The pilot noted that the airplane’s Continental C85 engine consumed 4.5 to 5 gallons per hour at a cruise power setting. The pilot reported that at 1602 the local flight departed Pelican Rapids Municipal Airport (47Y), Pelican Rapids, Minnesota. The pilot flew a meandering route over the lakes in the Pelican Rapids area, then over Highway 34 west to Barnesville, Minnesota, then to the south before turning back toward 47Y. The pilot reported that about 1 hour and 15 minutes had elapsed since departure when the airplane was on the left downwind for runway 33 at 47Y. The pilot acknowledged that the flight was 10 to 15 minutes longer than he had planned for, but the cork-and-wire fuel indicator gauge was about an inch above the empty indication. The pilot considered flying a circle-to-short final because there were no other aircraft in the traffic pattern; however, ultimately, he decided to fly a normal traffic pattern to runway 33. The pilot reported he reduced engine throttle and the airplane entered a descent during the turn from downwind to base leg. The airplane’s altitude and airspeed were reportedly lower-than-normal after the turn to base leg. The pilot increased the engine throttle but there was no response from the engine. The pilot reported that the engine continued to operate at a near idle power setting and at no point sputtered or quit. The airplane continued to descend rapidly toward trees. The pilot does not recall the final sequence of events that led to the impact with terrain. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the forward fuselage during the nose-low impact into a soybean field.
NTSB:20260929203890.s: The pilot of a Haberman Habercraft N10516 sustained minor injuries when the aircraft impacted terrain near Pelican Rapids, Minnesota, during the approach phase. The accident resulted from engine power loss due to fuel exhaustion, as the pilot failed to land despite the fuel gauge indicating near-empty levels.

NTSB:20260929203897.n: On September 29, 2026, about 0945 eastern daylight time, a special light-sport Costruzioni Aeronautiche Tecnam P92 Tail Dragger, N575TA, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Toughkenamon, Pennsylvania. The pilot was not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot reported that he had completed one takeoff and landing uneventfully on runway 24 at New Garden Airport (N57) Toughkenamon, Pennsylvania. After landing, he taxied the airplane off the runway and along a taxiway to initiate another takeoff on runway 24. As he neared the beginning of the runway, he initiated a right turn, but the movement of the airplane felt unusual, possibly due to a brake issue, and he stopped. He let the airplane roll and tried to turn right again, but the anomaly was still present, so he stopped again. Rather than continue to turn right onto the runway, he decided to turn left and taxi to a runup area where he could shut down the engine, exit the airplane, and inspect the landing gear. As he initiated the left turn, both main landing gear folded underneath the fuselage. Examination of the airplane by an FAA inspector revealed that it came to rest upright on the taxiway and sustained substantial damage to the fuselage. The inspector stated that the damage was consistent with the right main landing gear collapsing first, followed by the left. The right main landing gear strut was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260929203897.s: The pilot of a Tecnam P92 tail dragger, N575TA, substantially damaged the aircraft while taxiing at New Garden Airport after experiencing unusual handling during a right turn. Both main landing gear collapsed under the fuselage during a subsequent left turn, causing the aircraft to rest upright with damage consistent with the right gear failing first.

NTSB:20260930203904.n: On September 29, 2026, about 1828 central daylight time, a Cessna 152 II airplane, N69009, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Bolingbrook, Illinois. The flight instructor and the student pilot sustained minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight. The purpose of the local area flight was for the flight instructor to provide instruction to the student pilot, as part of JWA Flight School. JWA Flight School is based at the Bolingbrook’s Clow International Airport (1C5), Bolingbrook, Illinois. The airplane had a preflight inspection performed by both the flight instructor and the student pilot, and no abnormalities were noted. The student pilot was stationed in the left front seat, and the flight instructor was stationed in the right front seat. The airplane had about 24.5 gallons of 100 low lead fuel onboard for the flight. The engine runup process was completed and no abnormalities were noted. During the initial climb from runway 18 at 1C5, the student pilot who was manipulating the flight controls noted that “something was not right.” The flight instructor then immediately assumed the flight controls. She observed the tachometer and noticed that the engine RPM had decreased to about 20 RPM. She then executed the emergency procedure checklist and realized the airplane did not have sufficient engine power to climb due to the partial power loss, and the airplane was losing altitude. She performed a forced landing to a flat grass sports field in a residential area, about 0.25 miles southwest of the departure end of runway 18. The airplane came to rest upright in a nose-down profile on the grass field. During the impact sequence, the empennage separated about midspan. The student pilot was able to egress from the airplane on his own accord; however, the flight instructor was removed from the airplane by a bystander. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage, both wings, and the empennage. The airplane was recovered from the accident site and transported to a secure location for future examination. The airplane was manufactured in 1978. The airplane was equipped with a Lycoming Engines O-235-L2C reciprocating engine and a McCauley Propeller 1A103/TCM6958 fixed-pitch two-blade aluminum propeller. A review of the airplane’s maintenance records showed that an annual inspection was performed by a mechanic on July 23, 2026, for the airframe, the engine, and the propeller. Since the annual inspection occurred, the airplane had accumulated 40.9 hours. At the time of the accident, the airplane had accumulated a total of 14,851.9 hours. The flight instructor completed a flight review on April 24, 2025.
NTSB:20260930203904.s: During a Part 91 instructional climb from runway 18 at Clow International Airport, a Cessna 152 experienced partial power loss with engine RPM dropping to 20. The flight instructor executed a forced landing in a residential field, resulting in substantial damage and minor injuries to both occupants.

NTSB:20260930203906.n: On September 30, 2026, about 1410 central daylight time, a Cessna 525B, Dominican Republic registration HI1127, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident at Winston Field Airport (SNK), Snyder, Texas. The two pilots and one passenger were not injured. The airplane was operated by Panorama Jets as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 129 non-scheduled passenger flight. The flight departed from McClellan Airfield (MCC), Sacramento, California, at 0924 Pacific daylight time, on an instrument flight rules flight plan and proceeded to SNK at a cruise altitude of flight level 410 (FL410).
