The cockpit voice recorder (CVR) revealed that during the approach to SNK, which is a non-towered airport, the pilots received the SNK automated weather information four times. The reported weather was visual meteorological conditions, and the wind was generally from the south-southwest about 13 knots, gusting to 19 knots. The pilots received an approach clearance from air traffic control, then canceled their IFR flight plan and switched to the SNK common traffic advisory frequency. ADS-B data showed that the airplane’s transponder code changed from the assigned IFR code to 1200 at 1406:40, when the airplane was about 8 nautical miles (nm) south of the runway 35 threshold. The pilot-in-command (PIC), who was the pilot flying, reported that he selected runway 35 because it was the only runway with an instrument approach. Runway 17/35 is 5,599 ft long and 100 ft wide, with an asphalt surface. The company’s dispatch paperwork, which the pilots were referencing, included a runway analysis prepared at 1821 CDT the evening before the flight. The analysis was computed for landing on runway 17 using a forecast wind from 205° at 12 knots. It indicated “landing impossible” on runway 35 with that wind condition. ADS-B data showed that the airplane turned onto final approach for runway 35 at 1407, about 7 nm from the runway threshold. About 3 nm to the threshold, the airplane’s groundspeed was about 150 knots. The airplane crossed the runway 35 threshold at 1409:33 at a groundspeed of 149 knots, about 90 ft above the runway elevation. At 1409:40, the data indicated that the airplane was on the runway about 1,700 ft beyond the threshold, at a groundspeed of 138 knots. The groundspeed decreased to 80 knots at 1409:57, about 4,900 ft beyond the threshold, and then increased. The airplane passed the departure end of the runway at 1410:02 at a groundspeed of 92 knots, and it reached 104 knots about 400 ft beyond the runway end. Between 1410:07 and 1410:10, the groundspeed decreased from 104 to 54 knots, about 920 to 1,180 ft beyond the runway end. The final ADS-B position, at 1410:22, was about 1,415 ft beyond the departure end of runway 35 and about 60 ft left of the extended runway centerline. The PIC reported that the airplane landed within the first 1,000 ft. After touchdown, when he applied the main wheel brakes, the anti-skid system failed, and the airplane veered left of the runway centerline. He regained directional control and continued braking, but the airplane did not stop. He then initiated a go-around. The airplane departed the end of the runway, struck the airport perimeter fence and trees, and came to rest. The second-in-command (SIC), who was the pilot monitoring, reported that he selected the ground flaps after touchdown and that after braking began, the airplane moved alternately left and right of the centerline. He reported that takeoff power was applied and the ground flaps were retracted for the go-around, and that the airplane struck the fence and trees as it began to rotate. The pilots and passenger evacuated through the main cabin door without further incident. According to the airplane flight manual (AFM), for the airplane’s planned landing weight of about 10,500 lbs, the landing reference speed (VREF) was 99 knots, and the approach climb speed (VAPP) was 107 knots. The AFM landing performance tables did not include data for tailwind components greater than 10 knots. The PIC reported that he flew the final approach at 128 to 130 knots indicated airspeed (KIAS). The airplane came to rest in a tree line about 1,400 ft beyond the departure end of runway 35. The fuselage was partially separated from the wings and came to rest on its right side, while the wings remained level on the ground. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage and wings (see figure 1). Figure 1. Accident airplane where it came to rest in a tree line. The fuselage was partially separated from the wings and came to rest on its right side, while the wings remained level on the ground (Source: Snyder Police Department). At 1355, the SNK automated weather observation recorded wind from 200° at 13 knots gusting to 18 knots. At 1415, the wind was from 210° at 13 knots gusting to 18 knots. The CVR and flight data recorder (FDR) were sent to the NTSB Vehicle Recorder Laboratory for download. The airplane was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260930203906.s: Pilots of a Cessna 525B substantially damaged the aircraft during a landing at non-towered Winston Field Airport after the anti-skid system failed and the airplane overran the runway. The pilot initiated a go-around that resulted in a collision with a perimeter fence and trees due to high approach speed and tailwind conditions.

NTSB:20260930203907.n: On September 29, 2026, at about 1347 eastern daylight time, a Smith Pitts Special S-1, N292Y, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Madison, Georgia. The pilot was seriously injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to the pilot, on the day of the accident, he planned to fly from Madison Municipal Airport (52A), Madison, Georgia, to Atlanta Regional Airport-Falcon Field (FFC), Atlanta, Georgia to retrieve an airplane part. The pilot indicated the flight from 52A to FFC was uneventful, and after obtaining the airplane part, he departed for the return flight to 52A. Shortly after the pilot began his descent toward 52A, the airplane suddenly experienced a total loss of engine power. The pilot turned on the airplane's fuel boost pump, but when that failed to restore engine power, he began looking for a suitable area to perform a forced landing. As the pilot maneuvered the airplane toward a clearing, the engine briefly "revved up" two or three times before losing power again. The pilot subsequently performed a forced landing in the front yard of a residence. During the landing roll, the airplane impacted a tree, resulting in substantial damage to the wings and empennage. The pilot stated that, after he extracted himself from the airplane, he saw fuel pouring out of the airplane's fuel tank. The airplane was recovered to a secure storage facility for examination.
NTSB:20260930203907.s: The pilot of a Smith Pitts Special S-1, N292Y, suffered serious injuries after a total loss of engine power during descent to Madison Municipal Airport. The pilot executed a forced landing in a residence's front yard, where the aircraft struck a tree, causing substantial damage to the wings and empennage.

NTSB:20261001203908.n: On September 30, 2026, about 1946 Pacific daylight time, a Eurocopter Deutschland GMBH EC-135 P2+, N313RX, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Avalon, California. The pilot, flight nurse, and patient were fatally injured; the flight paramedic was seriously injured, and the passenger sustained minor injuries. The helicopter was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 135 air medical flight. The helicopter departed Pebbly Beach Seaplane Base (L11), Avalon, California, with a planned destination of Torrance, California. A review of ADS-B data revealed that the helicopter climbed to a maximum altitude of about 90 ft mean sea level. Shortly thereafter, the helicopter entered a descent for several seconds before it impacted water. The last data point indicated the helicopter's groundspeed was about 65 knots, and its descent rate was about 1,280 fpm. Witnesses near L11 reported that the helicopter lifted off from the seaplane base, entered a descent and then impacted water. The witnesses also noted that it was a dark, moonless night. A review of surveillance video revealed that a medical helicopter operated by another organization departed L11 about 45 seconds before the accident helicopter. The video showed that the helicopter lifted off from its helipad into a hover, turned and departed to the north. Approximately 13 seconds later the helicopter entered a descent, contacted the water twice, and then entered a climb. The accident helicopter then lifted off, climbed slightly and departed on a northerly heading. Several seconds later the helicopter entered a nose low attitude and subsequently impacted the water about 8 seconds later. The helicopter wreckage was located in the water, at a depth of about 209 ft, about 0.3 miles north of L11. The wreckage was recovered and retained for further examination.
NTSB:20261001203908.s: An EC-135 P2+ air medical helicopter crashed into water near Avalon, California, during night departure, killing the pilot, flight nurse, and patient. The aircraft entered a nose-low attitude shortly after liftoff and impacted the water at 65 knots with a descent rate of 1,280 fpm.

NTSB:20261001203910.n: On August 10, 2026, about 1800eastern daylight time, a Piper PA-24-250, N6985P, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Union City, Ohio. The flight instructor and the private pilot were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14?Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight. The flight instructor reported that he was giving a flight review to the airplane owner because the owner’s flight review was expired. Prior to the initial departure, an engine run-up was performed and “everything was normal.” The flight departed from Portland Municipal Airport (PLD), Portland, Indiana with about 55 gallons of fuel on board (nearly full) and proceeded to Randolph County Airport (I22), Winchester, Indiana, where a full stop landing was performed. The engine was secured before being restarted a few minutes later for another flight. Another engine run-up was performed with no discrepancies reported. The flight departed from I22 with the fuel selector position to the right fuel tank and the pilot climbed to 3,500 ft mean sea level where he performed air work for about 45 minutes. The flight instructor then asked the owner to come out of slow flight and go back to cruise flight. After leveling out of the turn the flight instructor reported that the engine “had a complete failure [but] the propeller was wind milling.” The flight instructor directed the owner to establish best glide airspeed, turn on the fuel auxiliary boost pump, and change the fuel selector to the left tank, which he did. While maneuvering for a nearby field the flight instructor “cycled the engine primer 4 times to get fuel to the engine…” but that did not restore engine power. At that time the airplane was at 200 ft above ground level and the owner lowered the landing gear. The airplane came to rest upright in the field with the nose and left main landing gear extended and the right wing resting on the ground. While the airplane was being recovered from the accident site, the left and right fuel tanks were drained, and contained about 12 gallons and 5 gallons of fuel, respectively. The recovery of the airplane was delayed due to the wet condition of the field. The airplane was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20261001203910.s: A flight instructor and private pilot in a Piper PA-24-250 experienced a complete engine failure at 200 feet AGL during an instructional flight near Union City, Ohio. The accident resulted in substantial damage after the pilot could not restore power despite switching fuel tanks and cycling the primer, though both occupants were uninjured.

NTSB:20261002203917.n: On October 1, 2026, about 1450 Pacific daylight time, an experimental amateur built Glasair FT airplane, N314SR, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Everett, Washington. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to friends of the pilot, before departure from Snohomish County Airport, Everett, Washington (KPAE) the pilot removed the upper and lower engine cowling to replace the exhaust gas temperature probe and Hobbs meter. FAA ADS-B data did not capture the accident flight. Video of the departure showed the airplane take off from runway 34L and begin rolling left almost immediately after liftoff. During the initial climb, the left bank continued to steepen until the airplane disappeared from view into trees west of the runway. A witness reported that the airplane initially appeared level and climbed at a normal rate. Within a few seconds, it entered a left bank that became substantially steeper than a normal departure turn. The witness estimated that the airplane climbed no higher than about 100 to 150 ft above ground level and described the turn as smooth rather than abrupt or erratic. The airplane remained in the banked turn until it disappeared behind trees. The witness did not observe the impact and did not recall unusual engine sounds, smoke, or components separating from the airplane before it disappeared from view. Another witness reported seeing the airplane about 50 to 60 ft above ground level in a steep left bank over the west side of the airport. The airplane continued in the banked turn until it disappeared into a wooded area. The controller reported hearing an unintelligible radio transmission that appeared to be from the pilot during the turn. The controller stated that the engine sounded normal before it disappeared from view. The main wreckage was located in a wooded area about 1,100 ft west of runway 34L and exhibited extensive impact and fire damage. The first identified point of impact was a tree crown that had separated about 75 ft above ground level, about 150 ft northeast of the main wreckage. The left wingtip was located beneath this tree strike, and additional material from the left wing was distributed between that location and the main wreckage. Both ailerons were present and exhibited thermal damage. Examination established flight control continuity from the control stick to the right aileron and to portions of the left aileron control system. An intermediate section of the left aileron push-pull tube had separated and was thermally damaged. The forward and aft wing spars were significantly damaged in that area. Elevator control continuity was established from the control stick to behind the seat. Thermal damage aft of that location precluded confirmation of continuity to the elevator. The rudder cables were continuous to the bell crank, which remained connected to the pushrod associated with the rudder. The flap handle was engaged in the third of four detents. The fuel selector handle was found in the wing tank position. The throttle and mixture controls were fully forward, the primer was pushed in and locked, and the ignition switch was in the BOTH position. The engine was rotated manually using the propeller. Rotational continuity to the magnetos and valve train movement were established, and thumb compression and suction were obtained on all four cylinders. Cylinder No. 1 was removed, and the exposed internal components exhibited no visible anomalies. Both magnetos exhibited thermal damage and water/foam intrusion; normal operation of both magnetos was not verified. The carburetor bowl was separated from the upper assembly, and the floats were deformed. The wreckage was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20261002203917.s: The pilot of an experimental Glasair FT was fatally injured when the aircraft entered a steep left bank shortly after takeoff from runway 34L at KPAE and impacted trees. The accident occurred following maintenance on the exhaust gas temperature probe and Hobbs meter, with the investigation noting a separated left aileron push-pull tube and thermal damage to the engine.

NTSB:20261005203929.n: The pilot purchased the airplane several days before the accident and was practicing some touch-and-go landings. After completing a successful touch-and-go landing, she was landing for a second time when the airplane bounced and veered off the left side of the runway. The airplane contacted a small dip in the grass and the nose landing gear collapsed resulting in substantial damage to the firewall and right wing. The pilot stated that there were no preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20261005203929.s: The pilot, practicing touch-and-go landings in a newly purchased airplane, bounced and veered off the runway during a second landing attempt. The nose gear collapsed after contacting a grass dip, causing substantial damage to the firewall and right wing, with no preimpact mechanical failures reported.

NTSB:20261005203932.n: On October 13, 2026, at 1412 mountain daylight time, a Socata TB 9 Tampico, N167GT, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Loveland, Colorado. The private pilot and a passenger were uninjured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot obtained full fuel and loaded the airplane with a passenger and baggage prior to departure for the personal flight. Air traffic control (ATC) cleared the flight for takeoff on runway 15 (8,500 ft by 100 ft, dry asphalt), which had a useable length of 3,750 ft due to construction at Northern Colorado Regional Airport. ATC instructed the flight to fly straight out and about ¾ down the runway, the airplane began to descend onto the closed portion of the runway. The airplane then impacted terrain as it exited the runway and sustained substantial damage to the left wing. The pilot stated that he was "pretty sure" there were no mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have preclude normal operation.
NTSB:20261005203932.s: A private pilot flying a Socata TB 9 Tampico sustained substantial left wing damage after the aircraft descended onto a closed runway section and impacted terrain during takeoff. The pilot reported no mechanical failures, attributing the accident to the aircraft exiting the reduced runway length due to construction.

NTSB:20261005203933.n: On October 2, 2026, about 1352 central daylight time, a Cessna 414A airplane, N1245A, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Boerne, Texas. The pilot and pilot-rated passenger were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 flight. According to the pilot, the airplane had just undergone its annual inspection which included the replacement of multiple engine cylinders, and this was the first flight after maintenance. During the takeoff roll from runway 17 at Boerne Stage Airfield (5C1), San Antonio, Texas, after passing 88 kts indicated airspeed, the pilot noticed that the left engine was not producing full engine power. The pilot determined that there was insufficient runway remaining to stop the airplane safely, he continued the takeoff. After the airplane lifted off from the runway, the pilot raised the landing gear and attempted to maintain control of the airplane with the maximum available engine power and an airspeed above the airplane’s minimum control speed (Vmca). The airplane struck a utility pole about 680 ft from the departure end of runway 17, subsequently igniting a fire from the right wing. The airplane impacted terrain and a post-impact fire ensued, destroying the airplane. The pilot and pilot-rated passenger egressed the airplane through the main cabin door. According to a witness, the airplane performed a static engine run on the maintenance ramp, and about 45 minutes later attempted a takeoff from runway 17. About 1,000 ft down the runway, the engine power was reduced to idle and the airplane exited the runway. During the second takeoff attempt, the witness observed the pilot apply full engine power, and about 1,000 ft down the runway, engine power was reduced to 50 percent. The witness observed the airplane become airborne and impact a powerline. The engines were recovered to a secure location for further investigation.
NTSB:20261005203933.s: The pilot of a Cessna 414A reported left engine power loss during takeoff from runway 17 at Boerne Stage Airfield shortly after cylinder replacement. The pilot continued the takeoff but the aircraft struck a utility pole and terrain, resulting in a post-impact fire that destroyed the airplane while both occupants escaped uninjured.

NTSB:20261005203934.n: On September 17, 2026, about 0710 mountain daylight time, a Piper PA18-150 airplane, N3879Z, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Karinen, South Dakota. The pilot was seriously injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to preliminary information obtained by responding FAA inspectors, the airplane impacted a field between two water tanks that the pilot checked every morning via aerial observation. Due to injuries, the pilot has not been able to provide additional information, and the time of the accident was approximated. The closest aviation reporting site, located about 24 nautical miles to the northeast, and about the estimated time of the accident, reported visibility less than 1/4 mile with moderate fog and an overcast ceiling at 200 ft. The airplane was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20261005203934.s: A pilot operating a Piper PA18-150 on a Part 91 flight was seriously injured when the aircraft impacted a field near Karinen, South Dakota. The accident likely resulted from reduced visibility due to fog and a low ceiling while the pilot conducted routine aerial observations.

NTSB:20261006203943.n: On September 26, 2026, about 1430 central daylight time, a Fairchild 24H, N16902, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Indianapolis, Indiana. The pilot and passenger were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. During the landing rollout shortly after the tailwheel settled to the ground, the pilot reported that the airplane drifted to the right. The pilot pushed the left rudder pedal and the left pedal felt stuck. The airplane departed the right side of the runway into the grass. It continued to the right hit a ditch and hill which resulted in the main landing gear collapse and substantial damage to the fuselage. Postaccident examination of the airplane revealed that a bent piece of metal, possibly a bellcrank travel stop, on the airplane's structure was making contact with the rudder bellcrank near the rudder pedals. Wear marks were present in the bellcrank that indicated the issue had been occurring for some time. The movement and contact between the two parts made a clicking noise and repeated movement of the rudder pedals resulted in the rudder bellcrank sticking during movement. Sometimes it would become lodged and require force to release the pedal. The airplane was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20261006203943.s: The pilot of a Fairchild 24H reported a stuck left rudder pedal during landing rollout near Indianapolis, causing the aircraft to drift right and depart the runway. Post-accident examination found a bent metal part contacting the rudder bellcrank, which caused the sticking and resulted in substantial damage after the plane hit a ditch.

NTSB:20261006203944.n: On October 4, 2026, about 2130 mountain daylight time, a Diamond Aircraft DA-40 airplane, N162GL, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Eldorado Springs, Colorado. The pilot and passenger were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. ADS-B data indicated that the flight departed from runway 29 at the Vance Brand Airport (LMO), Longmont, Colorado, about 1832. The pilot initially proceeded west and then south from LMO and maneuvered southwest of Boulder at altitudes up to 12,000 ft mean sea level (msl). He then flew about 68 miles to the northwest before reversing course, reaching altitudes of up to 15,000 ft msl during that portion of the flight. About 2036, the pilot returned to the vicinity of Boulder and maneuvered in that area between about 11,000 ft msl and 7,500 ft msl. The final ADS-B data point was recorded at 2129:39 and located about 1 mile north of Eldorado Springs. The altitude corresponding to that data point was about 7,375 ft msl. The Search and Rescue Satellite-Aided Tracking (SARSAT) network detected the airplane's emergency locator transmitter (ELT) signal at 2131. Notification of that signal was received by the Air Force Rescue Coordination Center (AFRCC) at 2132. The Boulder County Sheriff's Office was notified of the active ELT signal at 2143, and a search subsequently located the accident site about 1016 the following morning. The site was in mountainous terrain about 1 mile west of the final data point at an approximate elevation of 7,360 ft. The airplane impacted rising terrain about 300 ft below a ridgeline. The airframe was fragmented. Due to the difficulty of the terrain, and for safety reasons, the NTSB did not respond to the accident site. Airframe and engine examinations will be conducted after the wreckage is recovered to a secure location.
NTSB:20261006203944.s: A pilot and passenger were fatally injured when their Diamond DA-40, N162GL, impacted rising mountainous terrain near Eldorado Springs, Colorado, during a Part 91 personal flight. The aircraft was destroyed after the final ADS-B data point at 7,375 ft msl, with the ELT activating shortly before the crash.

NTSB:20261006203948.n: On October 4, 2026, about 1822 mountain daylight time, a Lancair IV-P-T airplane, N5UC, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Ontario, Oregon. The pilot and passenger were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to the pilot, the airplane departed Ontario Municipal Airport (ONO), Ontario, Oregon, destined for Provo Municipal Airport (PVU), Provo, Utah. During the initial climb, the airplane experienced a loss of engine power at an altitude of about 3,325 ft mean sea level. The pilot turned the airplane toward the departure airport, but then determined that he would be unable to reach the runway. He subsequently performed a forced landing in a field. While maneuvering to avoid a tree, the airplane's left wing contacted the ground. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage and left wing. The wreckage was retained for further examination. Figure 1 Accident site (Courtesy of Malheur County Sheriff's Office)
NTSB:20261006203948.s: The pilot of a Lancair IV-P-T, N5UC, experienced engine power loss at 3,325 feet MSL during initial climb from Ontario Municipal Airport. He performed a forced landing in a field, where the left wing struck the ground while avoiding a tree, causing substantial damage to the fuselage and wing.

NTSB:20261007203959.n: On October 7, 2026, at 0952 central daylight time, an Lancair IV-P airplane, N5SV, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Haslet, Texas. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) part 91 personal flight. A review of commercially available Automatic Dependent Surveillance Broadcast (ADS-B) data revealed that the flight departed Hicks Airfield (T67), Fort Worth, Texas, about 0951. ADS-B data showed that the airplane climbed to 875 ft mean sea level (msl) before it entered a left turn. The airplane climbed to 1,000 ft msl and slowed to 84 kts ground speed before it descended (Figure 1) Figure 1. N5SV Flight Track The airplane impacted power lines along the south side of a roadway. Fragments of composite propeller, fiberglass, and acrylic pieces were found under the power lines. An impact ground scar started about 3 ft from the north edge of the roadway and continued about 6 ft into an adjacent ditch. An impact crater along with fiberglass debris were located in the bottom of the ditch about 20 ft southwest of the main wreckage. Fire damage to grass and vegetation was observed upslope from the crater. The main wreckage came to rest upright on the north side of the ditch. It consisted of the fuselage, both wings, engine, and portions of the propeller. The fuselage was aligned along a true heading of 304°. A postimpact fire consumed a majority of the main wreckage. The horizontal stabilizer and elevator assembly separated from the aft fuselage and came to rest against a brick privacy wall north of the main wreckage. The vertical stabilizer and rudder assembly also separated from the aft fuselage and came to rest at the same privacy wall. The empennage exhibited no evidence of thermal damage. The wreckage was transported to a secure location for further examination.
NTSB:20261007203959.s: The pilot of a Lancair IV-P, N5SV, was fatally injured when the aircraft impacted power lines near Haslet, Texas, during a Part 91 personal flight. ADS-B data showed the airplane climbed to 1,000 ft MSL before descending and striking the lines, resulting in a post-impact fire that consumed the main wreckage.

NTSB:20261007203962.n: On October 7, 2026, at 1021 eastern daylight time, a Cessna 525 airplane, N600AL, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Bedford, Pennsylvania. One airline transport pilot sustained minor injuries, and the other airline transport pilot sustained serious injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 positioning flight. The flight crew reported that they arrived at the departure airport and the first officer completed a preflight inspection of the airplane. The crew reported that preflight, engine start, and taxi were uneventful. They continued that the airplane accelerated normally during the takeoff roll. The captain, who was the pilot flying, reported that during the takeoff roll the controls felt heavier than normal and as the airplane reached rotation speed it didn' t "fly itself off the ground." He then attempted to rotate and reported that the nose bounced at least once. The first officer reported that, during the takeoff roll, the captain stated he couldn' t lift the nose. The captain continued that the resistance on the yoke increased as the speed of the airplane increased. The captain subsequently made the decision to abort the takeoff and applied the brakes. The first officer stated that he deployed the speed brakes when the captain called for the aborted takeoff. The airplane departed the runway surface, crossed a grassy area, went through the airport perimeter fence, and came to rest in a field across from the airport. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage, both wings, and was partially consumed by postaccident fire. The airplane was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20261007203962.s: Two airline transport pilots operating a Cessna 525 on a Part 91 positioning flight aborted takeoff due to heavy controls and inability to rotate. The aircraft departed the runway, breached the perimeter fence, and sustained substantial damage with partial post-accident fire.

NTSB:20261008203971.n: On May 30, 2026, about 1832 mountain standard time, a Cirrus Design Corp SR20 airplane, N447AV, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Phoenix, Arizona. The flight instructor, student pilot, and passenger were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations instructional flight. The flight instructor reported that the airplane departed Phoenix Goodyear Airport (GYR), Goodyear, Arizona, and flew to Phoenix Deer Valley Airport (DVT), Phoenix, Arizona, to accomplish pattern work. The student pilot performed a normal landing and during the landing roll, when the nosewheel made contact with the runway, the nose landing gear collapsed. Postaccident examination revealed substantial damage to the airplane's firewall. Examination of the nose landing gear's oleo strut showed that an internal piston locking screw was missing. The strut had been replaced in February 2026, and the airplane had flown about 306 hours since replacement. The strut was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20261008203971.s: During a student landing roll at Phoenix Deer Valley Airport, a Cirrus SR20's nose gear collapsed upon nosewheel contact, substantially damaging the firewall. The flight instructor reported the accident was caused by a missing internal piston locking screw in the recently replaced oleo strut.

NTSB:20261012203978.n: On October 10, 2026, about 2014 Pacific daylight time, a Piper PA-18-150, N927JS, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Wauconda, Washington. The flight instructor and student pilot were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to the pilots’ family members, the student pilot had recently purchased the airplane, and had planned to fly the airplane from Willow Airport (PAUO) Willow, Alaska, to Kamiah Municipal Airport (S73), Kamiah, Idaho. According to an itinerary the student pilot had sent to family members, he anticipated it would take 3-4 days to fly from PAUO to S73. Both pilots booked commercial airline flights to Anchorage, Alaska, before departing PAUO on the morning of October 7, 2026. Between October 7 and October 9, the pilots performed several intermediate stops until they reached Prince George Airport (CYXS), Prince George, British Columbia, Canada, on the evening of October 9. At 0739 on the morning of the accident, the student pilot texted a family member, stating they were waiting for fog to lift before they departed. At 0808, he texted again, stating they were departing soon, but would have to divert around localized areas of fog. At 0914, he texted that they were departing CYXS. At about 1944, the student pilot sent a text indicating that they had landed at Dorothy Scott International Airport (0S7), Oroville, Washington, and were about to depart for the last leg of the flight to Kamiah Municipal Airport (S73), Kamiah, Idaho. According to preliminary air traffic control data provided by the FAA, one of the pilots of the accident airplane contacted Seattle Air Route Traffic Control Center (ZSE) to report they were about 10 miles south of 0S7 and were requesting flight following. The controller at ZSE provided the pilots with a transponder squawk code and asked about the flight’s destination. The pilots replied they were flying to Idaho County Airport (GIC), Grangeville, Idaho. About three minutes later, ZSE reported they had radar contact with N927JS about 20 miles southeast of 0S7 and asked for the airplane’s altitude. The pilots responded they were at 8,000 ft. About one minute later, ZSE attempted to reach the pilots because they had lost radar contact. The pilots did not respond, and no further radio transmissions were received from the airplane. When ZSE was unable to reestablish radar or radio contact with the airplane, the FAA issued an ALNOT. According to the Okanogan County Sheriff's Office, the airplane was located the following evening on the west face of Mount Annie, about 21 miles northeast of Omak, Washington. The main wreckage came to rest on forested, upsloping terrain at an altitude of about 5,069 ft above mean sea level. Examination of the accident site revealed a wreckage path that was about 225 ft long and generally oriented on a magnetic heading of 089°. The first identified points of contact (FIPC) were the tops of two tall fir trees which had been severed. About 120 feet east of the FIPC, sections of both wings were found about 40 feet above the ground, wrapped around the trunks of two fir trees. Both main landing gear, the inboard ends of both wings, freshly broken branches, and fragments of clear plastic were distributed along the ground near the end of the wreckage path. The main wreckage, which included the cabin, wing struts, engine, propeller, and empennage, came to rest nose down with the engine buried in the soil and the empennage folded down and to the right. The throttle levers were found positioned fully forward, the mixture knob was found in the full rich position, the primer pump was in and secure, the fuel selector was positioned to the right fuel tank, and the carburetor heat knob was set to off. An engine data monitor was removed from the airplane and retained for readout of any stored data. Further examination of the wreckage is pending following recovery.
NTSB:20261012203978.s: A flight instructor and student pilot were fatally injured when their Piper PA-18-150 crashed into Mount Annie, Washington, while flying from Oroville to Idaho. The aircraft lost radar and radio contact at 8,000 feet, and wreckage was found nose-down on forested terrain with throttle levers fully forward.

NTSB:20261013203989.n: On October 8, 2026, about 1400 central daylight time, a Mooney M20F airplane, N9068V, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Anderson, Indiana. The pilot was not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 flight test. The pilot reported that the purpose of the flight was to conduct a post-maintenance test flight. Shortly after takeoff, the pilot observed a pronounced left rolling tendency, and he decided to return to land at the airport. The pilot stated that during the approach the airplane was stable, but needed significant right aileron correction. After the main landing gear touched down, the airplane veered to the left, and the pilot was unable to regain control. The airplane exited the runway to the left and struck a taxiway sign, which resulted in substantial damage to the left wing. The airplane was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20261013203989.s: During a post-maintenance test flight of a Mooney M20F, the pilot encountered a left rolling tendency and significant right aileron correction needs shortly after takeoff. Upon landing, the aircraft veered left, exited the runway, and struck a taxiway sign, causing substantial damage to the left wing.

NTSB:20261013203995.n: On October 12, 2026, at 1540 central daylight time, a Piper PA-28-140 airplane, N9859W, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Abita Springs, Louisiana. The private pilot was uninjured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 91 personal flight. The pilot stated that he topped off the airplane fuel level for a personal flight that was to remain in the local area. He stated the engine runup for the flight was performed with a left fuel tank selection, the runup was normal, and he did not change fuel tank positions for the duration of the flight. He then performed two full stop takeoff and landings without incident prior to attempting a third takeoff. During the third takeoff roll and rotation, the engine instrument indications were normal. While the airplane climbed through 700 ft above ground level and entered a left turn for the downwind leg of the airport traffic pattern, the engine “sputtered.” The pilot stated that he verified the mixture control was in the full rich position and the fuel pump was on and “checked the carburetor heat with no apparent effect.” Shortly afterwards, the airplane experienced a total loss of engine power. The pilot stated that he engaged the engine starter, heard the starter operate, and saw the propeller turn, but the engine did not restart. He initially turned the airplane toward the departure runway but determined that the airplane would not have sufficient altitude to clear the trees along the return course. He identified an open field to his right, with a dirt road running through it, and selected that area for landing. During landing, the airplane impacted terrain and sustained substantial damage to the airplane’s left wing. The airplane owner stated that the airplane had not received a current annual inspection under CFR Part 91.409 at the time of the accident. The airplane was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20261013203995.s: A private pilot flying a Piper PA-28-140 experienced total engine power loss at 700 feet AGL during a local Part 91 flight, likely due to fuel exhaustion from not switching tanks. The pilot forced-landed in a field, sustaining substantial left wing damage, while the aircraft lacked a current annual inspection.

NTSB:20261019204026.n: On October 18, 2026, about 1500 central daylight time, a Piper J3C-65 airplane, N88218, was involved in an accident near Boonville, Indiana. The pilot was not injured and a passenger in a vehicle that was struck by the airplane was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 91 personal flight. The pilot reported that he departed from runway 9 at the Boonville Airport (I91), and shortly afterward returned to make a low approach to runway 27. He flew in ground effect until reaching the west end of the runway where he climbed, performed an “impossible turn,” and glided toward runway 9. He then applied full throttle when he was on short final for runway 9 and entered a climbing right turn to establish the airplane on a left downwind for runway 27. He then made a descending 180° turn to final approach. The approach was steep and carried the airplane down the runway. The pilot flew in ground effect with minimal throttle until about 2/3 of the way down the runway where he applied full throttle. He kept the airplane in ground effect as airspeed increased. When at the departure end of runway 27 and still at a low altitude, the airplane impacted a car traveling northbound on South Baker Road, which passed along the west edge of the airport. The pilot stated that he did not see the car traveling northbound until it was in front of him due to tall weeds, shadows cast on the road by trees, and the dark color of the car. He attempted to pull up to avoid the collision but was not able to. The airplane continued to fly, and the pilot circled the airport for about 2 hours before landing on runway 9. The pilot estimated that the airplane’s speed was about 70 mph at the time of the impact. The pilot reported no preimpact mechanical anomalies that would have precluded normal operation. The left main landing gear was separated from the airplane during the impact. The right side of the car was impacted and damaged. The passenger of the car, who was seated in the front right seat was transported to the hospital with serious injuries and later succumbed to those injuries. The driver of the car and the pilot were not injured.
NTSB:20261019204026.s: A pilot flying a Piper J3C-65 near Boonville, Indiana, struck a vehicle on South Baker Road while performing a low approach in ground effect. The collision occurred because tall weeds, shadows, and the car's dark color obscured the vehicle until it was too late to avoid impact, resulting in the passenger's death.

NTSB:20261019204030.n: On October 17, 2026, about 1030 Pacific daylight time, a Maule M-7-260, N3217V, was substantially damaged during a runway excursion while landing at The Sea Ranch Airport (CA51), Sea Ranch, California. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot had recently retrieved the airplane from a maintenance facility following an annual inspection and associated maintenance. During the initial engine run-up, the right wheel brake remained engaged after he released the parking brake. He re-engaged the parking brake and released it again, after which both brakes released normally. He then taxied the airplane and completed the flight to CA51 without further reported brake anomalies. According to the pilot, after touchdown, the airplane pulled strongly to the right. The pilot applied the left brake in an attempt to counter the turn, but was unable to maintain directional control. The airplane departed the right side of the runway, traveled through a drainage swale, and struck an embankment. The airplane sustained substantial damage to both wings and the right-wing struts. The pilot reported that he believed the right parking brake may have re-engaged after he checked the brake pedals before landing. The airplane was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20261019204030.s: The pilot of a Maule M-7-260, N3217V, lost directional control during landing at The Sea Ranch Airport (CA51) when the aircraft pulled right. The pilot attributed the runway excursion and substantial damage to a suspected re-engagement of the right parking brake.

NTSB:20261020204033.n: On October 15, 2026 at 1330 eastern daylight time, a Hughes 269C, N9655F, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Gastonia, North Carolina. The pilot was not injured. The helicopter was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight. The student pilot reported that he was practicing solo traffic pattern operations at Gastonia Municipal Airport (AKH), Gastonia, Georgia. Before touchdown on the fourth landing, less than 100 ft above ground level and less than 45 knots indicated airspeed, the pilot heard a loud bang. Immediately after, he heard the engine rpm increase and the rotor rpm decrease. The pilot continued and landed the helicopter hard on the runway. He reported that the helicopter's tail struck the ground, but that the helicopter landed upright on its skids. After exiting the helicopter, he observed that the clutch linear actuator was broken. A post-accident examination conducted by an FAA inspector revealed that the actuating shaft for the clutch linear actuator was fractured, and the cable that connected it to the helicopter's clutch assembly was no longer under tension. Substantial damage was observed to the helicopter's fuselage and tail rotor transmission. The wreckage was recovered and retained for further examination.
NTSB:20261020204033.s: A student pilot operating a Hughes 269C helicopter during solo traffic pattern practice at Gastonia Municipal Airport experienced a loud bang and loss of rotor RPM below 100 feet. The accident, caused by a fractured clutch linear actuator shaft, resulted in a hard landing with substantial damage to the fuselage and tail rotor transmission.

NTSB:20261020204036.n: On October 19, 2026, about 1703 central daylight time, a Consolidated Aeronautics Inc., Lake LA-4-200 airplane, N117RF, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Springfield, Missouri. The pilot and pilot-rated passenger received minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot reported that the airplane had been fueled about 30 minutes before he attempted to start the engine. He stated that when he engaged the engine starter, they heard and felt a large explosion from behind them. After several seconds, while shutting down the engine and airplane, they noticed dust and debris floating around them along with smoke. The pilot-rated-passenger also stated that their clothing was torn from the explosion. Video surveillance footage recorded shortly after the explosion showed light grey smoke emanating from the fuselage and both the pilot and pilot-rated-passenger were already outside of the airplane. The explosion and a subsequent interior fire resulted in substantial damage to the fuselage and empennage. Witnesses inside the nearby fixed base operator facility stated that the explosion rattled the building windows from about 300 ft away and was louder than a typical engine exhaust backfire. Postaccident examination of the fuselage hull revealed thermal damage to the interior structure of the lower right rear of the fuselage hull along with several burned electrical wiring bundles. Additional damage to the empennage hull and skin was observed with the skin being pillowed outward which was consistent with an overpressure event. The airplane was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20261020204036.s: During a Part 91 personal flight, a Consolidated Aeronautics Lake LA-4-200 suffered substantial damage when an explosion occurred behind the occupants upon engine start. The pilot attributed the event to a fueling issue 30 minutes prior, resulting in an interior fire that caused minor injuries and thermal damage to the fuselage and empennage.

NTSB:20261023204059.n: On October 22, 2026, about 1510 central daylight time, a Piper PA-28-160 airplane, N5393W, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Claremore, Oklahoma. The flight instructor and student pilot were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight. ADS-B data indicated that the flight departed from runway 18 at the Claremore Regional Airport (GCM) about 1431. The flight proceeded about 21 miles northeast of the airport at altitudes of up to about 3,500 feet mean sea level (msl). About 1455, the airplane reversed course and began to return to the airport. The final ADS-B data point was recorded at 1509:41 and was located about 2.08 miles east-southeast of GCM. The flight instructor reported that the student pilot leveled out at 2,500 feet to clear a tower about 5 miles east of the airport. After passing the tower, the student pilot continued the descent toward the airport traffic pattern. Shortly after reporting their position and intentions on the common traffic advisory frequency (CTAF), the engine lost power, although the propeller continued to windmill. Movement of the throttle control had no effect, and the flight instructor's efforts to restore engine power were unsuccessful. At that point, the flight instructor set up for and executed a forced landing to a field about 2 miles east-southeast of the airport. Upon touching down on the field, he attempted to keep the nose wheel off the ground as long as possible. However, once the nose wheel touched down, it dug into the soft ground and collapsed. The airplane came to rest upright with damage to the fuselage, left wing, and nose landing gear. Airframe and engine examinations are planned once the airplane is recovered from the accident site.
NTSB:20261023204059.s: During a Part 91 instructional flight in a Piper PA-28-160, the engine lost power at 2,500 feet while the student pilot descended toward the airport. The flight instructor executed a forced landing in a field, but the nose gear collapsed in soft ground, substantially damaging the aircraft.
